articles.title: L Catterton to invest in restaurant chain Nandhana Foods
articles.text:
L Catterton to invest in restaurant chain Nandhana Foods
The funding by global consumer focused investment firm L Catterton is expected to support Nandhana Foods' next phase of growth.
Global consumer-focused investment firm L Catterton has entered into a definitive agreement to invest in Nandhana Foods, a leading restaurant group specialising in South Indian cuisine. The value of the investment was not disclosed.
According to a statement, the investment will support Nandhana Foods’ next phase of growth and enable the group to achieve greater scale by leveraging L Catterton’s industry expertise and operating capabilities.
L Catterton Partner Vikram Kumaraswamy said, “Nandhana Foods’ founding family has built a distinctive and scalable business with a strong consumer proposition and attractive unit economics. It has expanded the business in a disciplined manner and ensured that its restaurants remain anchored in high quality and consistency.”
He also said, “We believe there is significant headroom for additional growth by further deepening and broadening its presence in South India and penetrating other markets. There is a clear path for prudently ramping up expansion.”
Founded in 2004, Nandhana Foods is a restaurant group that specialises in Andhra and Karnataka cuisine. It operates two brands, Nandhana Palace and RNR, and has 25 branches across Bengaluru and Chennai.
Nandhana Foods Founder and Managing Director R Ravichandar said, “We are pleased to partner with L Catterton, which has a track record of creating value for its portfolio companies across the world. The firm has a profound grasp of our organisational DNA and an intricate understanding of the restaurant industry.”
The statement said L Catterton has significant experience in building restaurant brands across the world.
The firm has invested in around 30 restaurant businesses till date. Its current and past portfolio companies include Dishoom, P.F. Chang’s, Velvet Taco, Baja Fresh, Cheddar’s Scratch Kitchen, Cigierre, HUGE, Impresario, and Mendocino Farms.
Founded in 1989, L Catterton manages around $40 billion of equity capital across multi-product platforms dedicated to private equity, credit, and real estate. It has made over 300 investments in consumer brands across the world.

articles.title: AI-based cyberattacks reshape cybersecurity - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Four insights you might have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of CrowdStrike’s Fal.Con
AI-based cyberattacks are now able to infiltrate an organization in seconds, leaving security teams next to no time to defend against intrusion.
This risk and CrowdStrike Holdings Inc.’s vision for helping organizations fight back were the focus of keynote remarks at CrowdStrike’s Fal.Con event by George Kurtz (pictured), president, chief executive officer and founder of CrowdStrike. AI has dramatically reduced the time it takes an attacker to move from an initial foothold within an organization to another target, a measure known as “breakout time,” according to theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante.
“Every year at this conference, George steps up and says breakout time has gone from two minutes to 72 seconds, down to 30 seconds,” Vellante said in an analysis of the day one keynote. “And now he’s like, it’s done. It’s just runtime. There is no breakout time.”
Here’s the complete Day 1 Keynote Analysis, part of SiliconANGLE’s and theCUBE’s coverage of Fal.Con:
CrowdStrike’s “2026 Global Threat Report” reported an average eCrime breakout time of just 29 minutes. The fastest attack took only 27 seconds , according to Michael Sentonas, president of CrowdStrike.
“I’ve never seen anything like it. I’ve never seen anything move so fast,” he said. “That’s all happening on one side. On the other side … I think it’s fascinating. It’s so exciting. There’s so much possibility. There’s so much we can do. Unfortunately, the benefit we get is also the benefit the attacker gets. That’s kind of that challenge that we have right now.”
At Fal.Con, CrowdStrike introduced its solution to this problem: SafeMind, a family of purpose-built security models created in partnership with Nvidia Corp. SafeMind is the first innovation from the CrowdStrike Cyber Superintelligence Lab, which the company is positioning as the first frontier AI research organization that’s using AI to stay one step ahead of AI-based threats, Kurtz noted.
“What we did is we created bespoke models that were built for defenders,” he said. “Oobviously we have an offensive model as well, which is needed. What we wanted to do was to give choice to customers.”
Here’s the complete video interview with Michael Sentonas:
Sentonas and Kurtz spoke with Vallante and host Rebecca Knight at Fal.Con, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. Along with experts from Amazon Inc., Nvidia, CISO Group, and other organizations, they discussed how the best defense could be AI that goes on the offensive. (* Disclosure below.)
Here are four key insights you may have missed from Fal.Con:
Insight #1: CrowdStrike bets on AI-powered red and blue teaming to harden defenses.
SafeMind aims to give defenders access to the same advanced AI capabilities attackers are using. That need drove CrowdStrike to develop security-specific models, explained Daniel Bernard, chief business officer of CrowdStrike.
“Frontier models have done a fantastic job bringing AI innovation to the market at large. It’s really benefited the adversary,” he said. “It’s time for the defenders to have something, and it’s time for security to have its own model. It turned into a set of models, a model family, and that’s where SafeMind was born.”
SafeMind consists of two AI models, Red Tempest and Blue Solano, trained on CrowdStrike incident data and built on Nvidia’s Nemotron family of AI models. Red Tempest hunts for attack paths by scanning a digital twin of the customer’s environment, explained Justin Boitano, vice president and general manager of enterprise computing at Nvidia. Blue Solano then fixes any vulnerabilities it finds.
“The digital twin describes the environment of the actual world,” he said. “You run the red agent through the environment and you’ll find different ways in to exfiltrate data. Then the blue agent will come in and write rules that would have detected or prevented the red attack agent from getting through. That iterative loop basically hardens the environment.”
Here’s the complete video interview with Daniel Bernard and Justin Boitano:
Insight #2: AI adversaries are shrinking the window to respond.
CrowdStrike’s research shows that speed is becoming one of the biggest challenges for security teams facing AI-driven threats. Such threats have increased dramatically over the past year, according to Adam Meyers, senior vice president of intelligence at CrowdStrike.
“The stat that’s most interesting is we had something like 26 agentic adversaries that we were tracking in the last 30 days,” he said. “That’s more than we were tracking in the year before that.”
Those agentic adversaries can move quickly. They operate far faster than human attackers, Meyers pointed out.
“In 58 minutes, VAULT PANDA had conducted 1,100 commands. It was an agent that was doing it, and we were watching it learn in real time,” he said. “When I talk about breakout time from our global threat report, we were talking this year about 29 minutes on average, 27 seconds was the fastest. I’m talking about an entire intrusion operation conducted in minutes from start to finish.”
Here’s the complete video interview with Adam Meyers:
Box Inc. uses CrowdStrike technology to help clients prevent intruders, including AI agents, from accessing sensitive corporate information. The technology strengthens protections for critical company data, according to Heather Ceylan, Box’s chief information security officer.
“Attack surface is the same, but it’s not just humans who are the attackers anymore,” she said. “It’s agents and they move at machine speed. So everything got faster. Our detections need to be faster, our visibility needs to be real time.”
AI sprawl further complicates the problem. Enterprises have rushed to deploy bots across their businesses without necessarily building the architecture needed to govern access and trust, added Cristian Rodriguez, field chief technology officer of the Americas at CrowdStrike.
“They’re calling us saying, we have a problem, the AI sprawl is real, we know it’s in our SaaS apps, we know it’s on our endpoints, we know it’s in our cloud instances,” he said. “[They are saying] help us get our arms around visibility and governance programs and control, because we’ve bitten off a little more than we can chew.”
Here’s the complete video interview with Cristian Rodriguez and Heather Ceylan:
Insight #3: AI is reshaping data loss prevention from the endpoint up.
Endpoint security remains an important focus for security teams focused on enterprise data loss prevention. Implementing on-device AI security can help prevent data loss when, for example, an employee pastes sensitive corporate information into a chatbot, said Todd Cramer, senior director of business development and security ecosystem at Intel Corp.
“This year, we have Falcon data security from CrowdStrike announcing their first AI model that runs on an Intel NPU on a Dell device,” he said. “It’s the right time in the use case, because we’ve got all these AI assistants, chatbots. What’s the first thing CISOs are worried about? Data.”
Dell Technologies is developing hardware telemetry solutions that give security teams full visibility into threats. The technology provides coverage across the entire technology stack, said Lori Zwilling, senior director of software product management at Dell Technologies Inc.
“Not only are analysts seeing the endpoint behavior, but they also can see what’s happening with AI models, the data, the inferencing, the actual containers, the compute that’s powering the AI for the enterprise,” Zwilling said. “We’re talking about full-stack AI security now.”
Here’s the complete video interview with Todd Cramer and Lori Zwilling:
AI is also changing how DLP identifies risky data movement. Jazz Inc. won the 2026 Cybersecurity Startup Accelerator from CrowdStrike and Amazon Web Services Inc. for its AI-based solution, which learns the business context surrounding risky outbound messages. AI-enabled DLP represents the evolution of a longstanding security challenge, according to Ido Livneh, co-founder and chief executive officer of Jazz.
“We didn’t build yet another pattern match or another rule-based system,” he said. “We completely upturned the whole challenge with our approach, which is building an investigator, a context-first, business-first investigator that understands your business, understands not only what is happening with the data flows, but why it’s happening, the intent, and solving it through that.”
Traditional DLP tools have often struggled to prevent data loss at scale. AI could help address that limitation by analyzing large volumes of information more effectively, said CJ Moses, chief information security officer and vice president of security engineering at Amazon.
“In my experience, DLP providers have never done what DLP actually, the acronym, stands for. They’ve never done the data loss prevention,” he said. “With basically AI now being a thing that actually will allow you to be able to deal with the large scale of the information and how they’ve implemented was kind of game changing for us.”
Here’s the complete video interview with CJ Moses, Ido Livneh, and Daniel Bernard:
Insight #4: An ecosystem strategy underpins CrowdStrike’s AI security push.
CrowdStrike is positioning SafeMind as the first major achievement of its Cyber Superintelligence Lab. The lab is developing technology intended to automate routine security tasks at the speed required to counter modern adversaries, CrowdStrike CEO Kurtz told theCUBE.
“Part of why we started the Cyber Superintelligence Lab is to be able to build these sort[s] of technologies so that we can get to a level of automation where the car drives itself,” he said. “Maybe the human has to be in the loop, and if something’s really critical, fine. If you can automate the most mundane task and you can do it with the speed at which the adversary is moving, that’s going to be critical.”
Here’s the complete video interview with George Kurtz:
The lab’s goal is to “disproportionately bias the advantage towards the defender,” according to Bartley Richardson, chief AI and autonomous systems officer at CrowdStrike.
“The real remit of the lab is the commoditization of defense capabilities. It is [turning] the best offense into that disproportionately advantaged defender-like capability,” Richardson told theCUBE. “How are we improving other areas in the industry itself? What can we contribute back?”
Here’s the complete video interview with Bartley Richardson:
Partnerships will also be key, as evidenced by CrowdStrike’s Project QuiltWorks, a cross-industry alliance of technology companies, law firms, consultancies, and others focused on finding and fixing security vulnerabilities surfaced by AI models.
“QuiltWorks is a coalition of folks and partners who join us; they leverage our platform,” explained Amanda Adams, senior vice president of global alliances at CrowdStrike, in an interview with theCUBE. “We announced yesterday Falcon IQ, and this is a tool built on AWS that allows a partner to essentially drive an assessment and highlight the opportunities, the priorities. It’s using AI to accelerate the time from discovery to remediation down to minutes.”
CrowdStrike’s partnership with Amazon Web Services has also evolved alongside the technology, according to Mona Chadha, director, strategic partnerships and category growth at Amazon Web Services Inc.
“Over the decade, what we continued to do was build innovations together,” Chadha told theCUBE. “We’ve evolved from machine learning to generative AI to now agentic and building these agents. There’s a lot of opportunity there, but there [are] also a lot of threats.”
Here’s the complete video interview with Mona Chadha and Amanda Adams:
Catch up on our complete video coverage of Fal.Con:

articles.title: Sur cette voiture électrique, le compteur de vitesse disparaît sur la version de base
articles.text:
Sœur technique de la Kia EV4, la Hyundai Ioniq 3 adopte un style différent mais tout aussi original. Cette compacte électrique vient naturellement chasser sur les terres des Renault Mégane et autres Volkswagen ID.3 Neo. Mais en débutant sous les 30 000 € grâce à une petite batterie de 42 kWh, la coréenne part avec un avantage tarifaire certain. Si l’autonomie est moindre, ce ne sera pas le seul compromis à faire pour bénéficier d’un prix attractif.
La version de base Select à 29 995 € fait l’impasse sur les vitres surteintées, les essuie-glaces automatiques, le préconditionnement de la batterie, les sièges avant chauffants et les rétroviseurs rabattables électriquement. Ce n’est pas un drame pour une version premier prix. En revanche, on note une absence bien plus dérangeante : l’instrumentation derrière le volant, qui disparaît complètement.
Le grand absent de l’habitacle : où est passé le compteur ?
Le petit rectangle numérique placé sur la planche de bord donnait pourtant des informations bien utiles comme l’autonomie, le niveau de batterie, les indications du GPS, les limitations de vitesse et… la vitesse. Un peu embêtant, surtout que la version de base n’a évidemment pas d’affichage tête haute. Vous pourrez bien entendu toujours lire votre vitesse, mais il faudra déporter votre regard vers l’écran central comme chez Tesla.
Et si vous avez une électrique de la marque californienne, vous vous sentirez vraiment comme à la maison puisque c’est la zone de gauche qui est entièrement dédiée au véhicule. Vous retrouverez ainsi la vitesse, les voyants, l’autonomie, la position du variateur et l’état général de la voiture. Que se passe-t-il alors si vous choisissez les versions supérieures équipées de l’instrumentation de 9,9 pouces ?
Un compteur facturé au prix fort : l’addition salée de la finition supérieure
Pas grand-chose, si ce n’est que vous aurez tout affiché en double… C’est étrange, mais c’est bien le choix fait par Hyundai. Ceux qui ne pourront se passer d’instrumentation traditionnelle ne pourront d’ailleurs pas se procurer cet équipement en option sur la version Select. Il faut forcément passer au niveau supérieur Trend à 32 300 € pour retrouver cet affichage plus classique. Le gap de 2 305 € est non négligeable sur ce genre de véhicule…
Mais ce compromis demeure tout de même très acceptable car l’ID.3 Neo démarre à 34 990 € alors que la Mégane attaque à 37 500 €. La dotation de la coréenne est en plus toujours appréciable, ce qui la rend plutôt compétitive. La batterie de 61 kWh, elle, est accessible contre 33 995 €. La nouvelle Hyundai Ioniq 3 est d’ores et déjà disponible à la commande. Les essais suivront au mois d’octobre.

articles.title: SpaceX declares Starship ready for orbit, sets launch date next week
articles.text:
Pending regulatory approval, SpaceX said today it intends to launch its 14th Starship mission as early as September 22. This flight is notable, as it will be the first time that SpaceX attempts to launch the experimental vehicle into orbit.
The company set a target liftoff time of 7:15 am local in Texas (12:15 UTC), with a 75-minute launch window. Sunrise in Brownsville, Texas, is 7:17 am CT, so the launch could make for some striking imagery.
The super heavy lift rocket will be carrying 26 of the larger V3 Starlink satellites into an orbit 275 km above the Earth. In an update on its website, SpaceX said the Starship upper stage will seek to complete six orbits around the Earth before completing its mission after about 10 hours.
Reaching orbit would mark a significant milestone in the company’s Starship development campaign, which conducted its first test flight on April 20, 2023, and has since made progress in fits and starts. With the upcoming mission, SpaceX continues to make modifications to the Starship vehicle as it seeks to improve the third iteration of the Super Heavy booster and Starship upper stage. After recent successes, the company appears to be closer to developing a fully reusable, super heavy lift rocket.
First-stage modifications
During the most recent Starship test flight on July 24, the vehicle’s first stage performed nominally during ascent. However, after a successful boostback burn, the vehicle experienced problems during the return through Earth’s atmosphere.
“In the terminal phase of the burn, the three center engines showed signs of ice clogging, which triggered an early end to the maneuver,” SpaceX said in its update on Tuesday. “The booster went on to attempt a landing burn, with 8 of the 13 planned engines reigniting before the booster made a hard splashdown in the Gulf. The Super Heavy on this upcoming flight has hardware modifications to improve filtering to the engines and software changes to enhance relight reliability.”

articles.title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says ‘the world is right to be afraid’ of AI influence — but that it can benefit humanity like no other technology before it
articles.text:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says ‘the world is right to be afraid’ of AI influence — but that it can benefit humanity like no other technology before it
Sam Altman reflects on “insane mission” of OpenAI, and where the tech will go next
- Sam Altman admits AI development may require greater control
- Altman references Hugging Face "accident" as something which might cause wider distrust
- However Altman said he still believes AI technology can greatly benefit humanity as a whole
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has admitted that the rapid pace of development in the AI industry is rightfully scaring some people, and that more controls might be necessary.
Speaking at Dreamforce 2026, Altman was quizzed by Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff on a variety of topics, giving his opinion on not just the most recent incidents in the world of technology, but where the future of AI could go next.
"This could go wrong"
Altman and Benioff's wide-ranging conversation began with the latter asking the former for his view on "what's been going on" concerning recent controversies in the AI industry.
This included the widely-reported Hugging Face hack, as well as increasing calls for greater AI regulation in recent weeks.
"People have been talking about the potential downsides or serious risks of AI for some time,” Altman said, noting that the increased capabilities of models have meant people are paying more attention than ever before.
Altman also highlighted the recent “Hugging Face accident”, which he later described as “obviously a terrifying incident”, as raising awareness among the wider world as to what AI is capable of.
“It doesn't take as much imagination as it used to, to imagine how this could go wrong,” he pointed out, adding that he would like to know that companies don’t intend to use their models for nefarious means - “there should be no qualifier on that,” he pointed out.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Altman also highlighted the “real fear” that “some companies working in AI could get too much power and be able to influence the economy”.
“I think the world is right to be afraid of this,” he pointed out.
Future hopes
However it wasn’t all doom and gloom, as Altman noted that OpenAI was navigating a “narrow path” with pragmatism, steadiness and consistency.
“People are now saying, this seems pretty important, so let's get it right...and we will get it right, by the way, I'm very confident in our ability to do this. The world should trust that we are going to do the right thing, because it is the right thing, and we know the magnitude of this.”
Altman was also confident that despite the continuing advances of AI, he had high hopes for the future of humanity, noting that while "people don't care that much what a machine does...we have a wonderful ability of being obsessed with other people.”
However this might still involve some tough work, as society and people would “need to uplift themselves very fast” to get all the advantages of technology - “but this seems very achievable to me,” Altman added.
Looking forward
Overall though, Altman noted that the degree that people care about other people is a major positive, and predicted that "we will stay in an extremely human-centric world, no matter what technology does.”
AI will help with this progress, though, with Altman saying that although the technology is capable of incidents such as the Hugging Face hack, it is also possible to use AI to defend against such attacks.
“We have to (use AI to defend) to get the prize of curing diseases, giving people this incredible creativity, this human entrepreneurship that I think is coming.”
“I think people, with this technology in their hands, can live a much better version of their lives.”
Benioff closed out the session by asking what he hoped the legacy of his company would be, with Altman noting that the company had set out on an "insane mission" to achieve AGI, and that it had only scratched the surface" of building great products".
“There is no doubt there will be more technological wonders by 2030, and they'll be big ones,” he added, highlighting the fact that you can talk to a computer and it knows what you want, understand your company and take action, “is one of the most profound changes to how we use technology that I've ever seen...this is one of the moments that feels like you're in a movie (and) I think this will transform the way we work and use computers”.

articles.title: US AI data centers projected to become the fifth-largest natural gas consumer in the world by 2035 — consumption to grow by 15 billion cubic feet per day as demand for compute increases
articles.text:
US AI data centers projected to become the fifth-largest natural gas consumer in the world by 2035 — consumption to grow by 15 billion cubic feet per day as demand for compute increases
Only China, Russia, Iran, and the U.S. itself are expected to use up more of this fossil fuel.
The estimated natural gas consumption of data centers in the U.S. is expected to massively increase as these facilities increasingly rely on gas turbine generators for their power. According to Bloomberg, data centers are projected to use up to 15 billion cubic feet per day by 2035, a 117% increase from the previous forecast of 6.9 billion cubic feet. This number tracks with other data center forecasts, which suggest that data centers will use 20% of U.S. power by 2035, amounting to about 194 gigawatts.
Many data center projects have already been delayed by the lack of available power infrastructure, with power plants expected to take so much longer before they come online. It’s for this reason that many developments have turned towards onsite generators, so much so that AI demand is now compounding the jet engine shortage already plaguing the aviation industry.
Elon Musk was among the first to use gas turbines to power a data center when he deployed them at the Memphis Supercluster in 2024, even though he didn’t have permits for some of them. Now, it seems that the world’s richest man has seen this trend and has invested a billion dollars to buy a portable gas and diesel turbine leasing company. He even announced that SpaceX will start in-house turbine blade manufacturing to help cut down on the manufacturing bottleneck plaguing the jet engine industry.
New technologies like small modular reactors are currently being developed as an answer to AI data centers’ insatiable demand for power, like Ampera’s 3D-printed modular thorium nuclear reactor or Valar Atomics’ Ward 250 nuclear microreactor. Many AI hyperscalers, including Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Nvidia, and Oracle, have even invested in projects like these in a bid to generate massive amounts of clean energy for AI. However, they’re expected to take a few more years before they could become commercially viable — time that tech giants do not have. Because of this, Musk said that “natural gas will still be needed to supplement and bootstrap solar for several years.”
The deployment of natural gas turbines in data centers isn’t good news for the communities living around them, though. The NAACP said in its lawsuit against SpaceXAI that the use of these turbines at Colossus 2 increased nitrogen oxide exhaust by 111%, PM2.5 particles by 83%, and formaldehyde emissions by 88%. While the company has already pledged to remove all its unpermitted generators, the process will take at least a year as the portable turbines are slowly being replaced by a 1.2-gigawatt on-site power plant.
Aside from this, the massive demand for natural gas could potentially put a strain on the supply, causing prices to rise and hit the average consumer. Domestic natural gas producers are projected to raise their output by 35 billion cubic feet per day in the next decade, but this still falls short of the forecasted demand by around 11 billion cubic feet per day. So, unless output manages to catch up with the demand, prices are expected to shoot up and cause a scramble for available supply. Still, some experts suggest that there are still more than enough undeveloped gas fields within the U.S. to allow the industry to increase natural gas supplies and reduce costs.

articles.title: Boston dumps Flock, says it shared data nationwide in violation of contract
articles.text:
The Boston city government abandoned Flock Safety’s license-plate reader cameras after the company shared data nationwide in violation of a contract provision, according to city officials.
“We have actually abandoned Flock,” Boston Mayor Michelle Wu said in her monthly “Ask the Mayor” segment on GBH News last week. Wu made the comment a few days before the release of Boston’s annual surveillance technology report, which said a Flock “vendor error” resulted in nationwide data sharing.
The report, which covers 2025, describes how the Boston Police Department deployed about 45 Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) cameras in a trial with Flock from April to September last year. The unauthorized data sharing occurred during the first few days of the pilot, the report said:
Pursuant to the contract, the Flock ALPR Pilot Program was designed to restrict access to the data collected by BPD ALPR cameras exclusively to trained BPD personnel. The contract clearly noted that data sharing was to be disabled, and BPD confirmed with Flock that settings were “off” for sharing. Within three days of initiating the Pilot, BPD became aware that other law enforcement agencies were able to access license plate and vehicle information collected from BPD ALPR cameras using a nationwide lookup feature that was enabled by the vendor in error. Upon learning of the vendor error, BPD ensured that the function was immediately disabled and access to the Department’s data was no longer available without submitting a written request to BPD as described above. No further direct access was available for the duration of the Pilot.
The report didn’t say how many law enforcement agencies accessed the data. The problem with Flock didn’t stop Boston from seeking another vendor of license-plate reader technology. The police department started another license-plate reader trial with Motorola in February 2026 and a third trial with Axon in June 2026.
Boston’s report comes amid a larger privacy debate over law enforcement access to license-plate camera data. An Electronic Frontier Foundation report yesterday described how the nationwide lookup tool lets police conduct searches with little or no justification.

articles.title: 7 Roald Dahl quotes that reveal life's biggest lessons
articles.text:
7 Roald Dahl quotes that reveal life's biggest lessons
Discover 7 Roald Dahl quotes that reveal powerful lessons about kindness, courage, imagination, and living a meaningful life.
Roald Dahl is best known for creating magical worlds filled with giant peaches, chocolate factories, friendly giants, and extraordinary children.
While his stories are often shelved as children's literature, many of his most memorable lines contain wisdom that resonates just as deeply with adults.
Beneath the humour, adventure, and imagination lies a collection of life lessons about kindness, courage, resilience, and the importance of staying true to yourself.
Part of what makes Dahl's work timeless is his ability to express profound truths in simple, memorable ways. His characters face bullies, overcome obstacles, and discover the power of curiosity and kindness. These themes continue to inspire readers decades after his books were first published.
7 Roald Dahl quotes that reveal some of life's biggest lessons
1. “A person who has good thoughts cannot ever be ugly.”
This memorable quote from The Twits reminds readers that true beauty comes from within. Roald Dahl believed that kindness, generosity, and a positive outlook shape how others see us far more than physical appearance ever could.
In a world obsessed with looks and perfection, the quote offers a refreshing lesson. Character, compassion, and the way we treat people leave a lasting impression. While appearances may change over time, a good heart and kind spirit have the power to make someone truly beautiful.
2. “Never grow up... always down.”
This playful quote reflects Roald Dahl's belief that adults should never completely lose the curiosity, imagination, and sense of wonder they had as children. Throughout his books, the most memorable characters are often those who remain open-minded, adventurous, and willing to see magic in ordinary things.
The quote serves as a reminder that growing older does not have to mean becoming cynical or unimaginative. Keeping a childlike sense of curiosity can help people stay creative, adaptable, and excited about life. Some of life's greatest discoveries happen when we continue to ask questions, explore new ideas, and embrace the world with fresh eyes.
3. “A little magic can take you a long way.”
While Dahl's stories are filled with fantastical elements, this quote speaks to something very real: the power of imagination.
Life can become routine and predictable, but imagination allows people to dream, innovate, and see possibilities where others see limitations. Whether through creativity, optimism, or curiosity, a little "magic" often helps people navigate challenges and discover new opportunities.
4. “Never do anything by halves if you want to get away with it. Be outrageous. Go the whole hog.”
This humorous quote reflects Dahl's appreciation for boldness and enthusiasm. While it is delivered with characteristic wit, it contains an important lesson about commitment.
Success often requires full effort and genuine dedication. Whether pursuing a goal, developing a skill, or chasing a dream, half-hearted attempts rarely produce extraordinary results. Dahl encourages readers to embrace life with energy and conviction.
5. “The more risks you allow your children to make, the better they learn to look after themselves.”
Although written about children, this quote contains wisdom for people of all ages. Growth often requires stepping outside comfort zones and learning through experience.
Mistakes and setbacks are not signs of failure; they are opportunities to learn. By embracing challenges rather than avoiding them, individuals develop confidence, resilience, and independence.
6. “Life is more fun if you play games.”
This simple yet powerful quote reflects one of Roald Dahl's favourite themes: the importance of imagination, playfulness, and not taking life too seriously. Throughout his stories, characters often find joy and adventure by embracing creativity and seeing the world differently.
As adults, it's easy to become consumed by responsibilities and routines. Dahl's words serve as a reminder that happiness often comes from maintaining a sense of fun, curiosity, and spontaneity. Life may be filled with challenges, but approaching it with a playful spirit can make the journey far more enjoyable.
7. “A little nonsense now and then, is relished by the wisest men.”
This witty quote reminds readers that life is not meant to be taken all the time seriously. Roald Dahl understood that humour, playfulness, and moments of silliness are just as important as hard work and responsibility.
In a world that often celebrates productivity and achievement, the quote encourages people to make room for joy. Whether it's laughing with friends, pursuing a hobby, or simply embracing life's absurd moments, a little nonsense can bring balance and happiness. Sometimes, wisdom is not about being serious all the time; it's about knowing when to enjoy life and have fun.
Why Roald Dahl's quotes still matter
Roald Dahl's stories continue to captivate readers because they explore universal truths through imagination. His books celebrate courage over fear, kindness over cruelty, and curiosity over conformity.
Though written for children, Dahl's quotes offer insights that remain relevant to adults. They encourage readers to stay curious, embrace imagination, face challenges with courage, and believe in their ability to make a difference.
Perhaps that is why his stories endure. Long after the final page, their lessons continue to inspire wonder, kindness, and optimism.

articles.title: Dissidents et journalistes piégés par un faux Norton aux mains des Iraniens
articles.text:
Sous couvert d'un faux installateur Norton Antivirus ou de résultats d'IRM falsifiés, des pirates informatiques liés à l'État iranien traquent des dissidents, des activistes et des journalistes partout dans le monde. Le logiciel espion CHOSEN BRICK infecte alors leur ordinateur Windows, capture leur écran, enregistre leur microphone et vide leurs messageries Telegram et WhatsApp.
Le ministère iranien du Renseignement et de la Sécurité (MOIS) est à l'origine de cette campagne, selon une alerte conjointe publiée par le NCSC britannique, le FBI américain et l'AIVD néerlandais. Un correspondant usurpe l'identité d'une relation déjà connue de la cible ou celle d'un support technique, sur WhatsApp ou Telegram. Comme le rapporte notre confrère PC Mag, il transmet ensuite un fichier déguisé en Norton Antivirus, en une autre application légitime, ou en résultat d'examen médical. Une fois le fichier ouvert, CHOSEN BRICK prend pied sur l'ordinateur Windows de la victime. Le logiciel espion cible, depuis au moins 2025, des dissidents, des activistes et des journalistes critiques du régime iranien, au Royaume-Uni, aux États-Unis, aux Pays-Bas et dans plusieurs autres pays.
Persistance et contournement de Windows Defender
Les opérateurs mènent une recherche poussée sur la cible avant tout contact, puis la poussent à basculer d'un appareil professionnel vers un appareil personnel, hors de portée des contrôles de sécurité de son entreprise. Les installateurs falsifiés ne visent que les postes Windows. Selon les trois agences, aucune variante pour macOS ou pour les smartphones n'a pour l'instant été recensée.
Après son installation, CHOSEN BRICK inscrit une clé dans le registre Windows, sous HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run.
Cette clé relance CHOSEN BRICK à chaque démarrage de Windows, sans fenêtre visible pour l'utilisateur, si bien que le logiciel espion échappe plus longtemps aux outils de détection.
CHOSEN BRICK ajoute ensuite ses fichiers aux exclusions de Windows Defender. L'antivirus de Microsoft ne les analyse alors plus.
CHOSEN BRICK communique enfin avec ses opérateurs par un robot Telegram doté d'un identifiant unique pour chaque victime.
Un espionnage tous azimuts
Une fois actif, CHOSEN BRICK dresse la liste des processus et des informations système de l'ordinateur infecté. Ces informations aident les opérateurs à choisir les logiciels malveillants complémentaires à déployer par la suite.
Le logiciel espion capture aussi l'écran, enregistre l'audio du microphone et récupère les messages Telegram et WhatsApp ainsi que les e-mails de la victime. Les captures d'écran et les enregistrements audio empruntent eux aussi le canal Telegram déjà utilisé pour la commande à distance. CHOSEN BRICK récupère en outre le carnet de contacts de la victime. Les opérateurs identifient ainsi son entourage proche.
À la demande de ses opérateurs, CHOSEN BRICK télécharge des logiciels malveillants supplémentaires ou supprime des fichiers. Les données volées transitent par Telegram ou par les services de stockage cloud VultrObjects et StorjShare.
Le MOIS visé par une alerte inédite à trois pays
Le FBI précise que le MOIS utilise CHOSEN BRICK pour collecter du renseignement, provoquer des fuites de données et porter atteinte à la réputation de ses cibles. « Les détails de cette campagne cybernétique montrent que l'Iran utilise impitoyablement la surveillance numérique pour réprimer les critiques du régime, en volant des e-mails et des messages et en accédant aux appareils », a déclaré Paul Chichester, directeur des opérations du NCSC britannique.
Pour le gouvernement britannique, ce type d'opérations s'apparente à de la répression transnationale. Un État cherche à réduire au silence, au-delà de ses frontières, des personnes hostiles à son pouvoir.
Le Royaume-Uni, les États-Unis et les Pays-Bas recommandent aux personnes exposées de maintenir leurs appareils à jour, de garder un antivirus actif et de ne jamais ignorer les avertissements de SmartScreen. Les administrateurs réseau sont invités à déployer une authentification résistante au hameçonnage, à restreindre l'installation de logiciels aux seules applications autorisées et à filtrer les pièces jointes reçues par e-mail. Les particuliers les plus exposés peuvent aussi trouver des services de défense cybernétique gratuits auprès du NCSC britannique, ainsi qu'un guide gouvernemental consacré à la répression transnationale sur le site gov.uk.

articles.title: GraphSummit introduces Neo4j as context layer for agents - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
What to expect at Neo4j’s GraphSummit: Join theCUBE Sept. 24
Enterprises are facing a context problem — and models alone are not enough to solve it.
Graph databases, which connect data with intelligent context that models and agents can better understand, are becoming a critical part of application development. Neo4j Inc., a leader in graph technology, is focused on supporting developers with its AI-powered graph solutions.
“From an AppDev perspective, the value of technologies such as Neo4j is that they give developers a way to represent the relationships, dependencies and business context that AI applications need to reason effectively,” said Paul Nashawaty, principal analyst for theCUBE. “Moving from experimentation to production requires more than embedding an LLM into an application. It requires trusted, connected data that AI can retrieve, understand and act upon.”
This month’s GraphSummit will feature leaders and experts in graph technology, with an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. Don’t miss theCUBE’s event coverage to learn more about Neo4j’s role in the agentic AI era and the evolution of graph systems. (* Disclosure below.)
Building intelligent context into agentic AI
TheCUBE’s AppDev research shows that 90% of enterprises are actively adopting AI agents but an approximately 30% operational-readiness gap remains between AI experimentation and production-scale deployment, according to Nashawaty. Neo4j’s graph solutions are intended to close that gap by giving agents consistent context across different systems.
“As agents move from copilots that answer questions to systems that take action, the ability to understand what is connected to what, why that relationship matters and what actions are safe becomes foundational,” Nashawaty said. “That makes the graph less of a specialized database technology and more of a potential knowledge layer for the next generation of enterprise applications.”
Neo4j is now building Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation directly into its developer workflow. GraphRAG combines vector search with relationship-aware retrieval, enabling agents to understand business context and provide a more traceable basis for their decisions.
The company’s recent acquisition of GraphAware further points to its ambitions as an intelligence layer for agentic AI. While Neo4j is not a direct competitor for Palantir, it does provide an alternative to Palantir Gotham, a data analysis and decision-making platform, Nashawaty pointed out.
“Neo4j is positioning the graph as a knowledge and reasoning layer for AI applications, while Palantir’s Ontology is more tightly coupled to its broader operational platform,” he said. “Neo4j’s acquisition of GraphAware and its explicit positioning as an open-standard alternative to Palantir Gotham, however, shows that the company is moving beyond being a database provider and directly into intelligence and AI-driven decision support.”
TheCUBE event livestream
Don’t miss theCUBE’s coverage of GraphSummit on Sept. 24. You can also access theCUBE’s exclusive content on demand after the event broadcast.
How to watch theCUBE interviews
There are several ways to follow theCUBE’s coverage of GraphSummit, including theCUBE’s dedicated website and YouTube channel. You can also find coverage from theCUBE events on SiliconANGLE.
TheCUBE podcasts
SiliconANGLE’s “theCUBE Pod” is available on Apple Podcasts, Spotify and YouTube, making it easy to follow the program on the go. During each podcast, SiliconANGLE’s John Furrier and Dave Vellante unpack the biggest trends in enterprise tech — from AI and cloud to regulation and workplace culture — with exclusive context and analysis.
SiliconANGLE also produces our weekly “Breaking Analysis” program, where Dave Vellante examines the top stories in enterprise tech, combining insights from theCUBE with spending data from Enterprise Technology Research. The program is available on Apple Podcasts, Spotify and YouTube.
Guests
During theCUBE’s coverage of GraphSummit, our analysts will talk with leaders and experts from Neo4j, Dell Technologies, Blitzy, Collibra, Qiagen, Raymond James, and more, about graph technology, connected data and the knowledge layer for enterprise AI.

articles.title: España se ha situado en la cabeza de Europa en algo: el esfuerzo acumulado desde los años 80 para comprarse una vivienda
articles.text:
A lo largo de los último 45 años los españoles hemos visto cómo aumentaban nuestras rentas y cómo se disparaba el precio de la vivienda, más o menos igual que el resto de nuestros socios comunitarios. El problema es que esos dos valores (el dinero del que disponen las familias y la cotización del m2) no han avanzado al mismo ritmo. Al contrario. El primero lo ha hecho a mucha menos velocidad que el segundo, exigiendo un mayor sacrificio por parte de las familias y generando una brecha que nos aleja cada vez más de la media europea.
Los datos el Banco de España son demoledores.
¿Qué ha pasado? España tiene un problema con la vivienda. Lo reconoce el Gobierno y lo constatan las estadísticas que, cada poco, nos recuerdan la espiral alcista de sus precios. Una de las últimas de hecho es la del Consejo General del Notariado (CGN), que muestra que aunque el mercado inmobiliario se está enfriando la vivienda sigue encareciéndose, escalando a valores históricos.
Lo que resulta más difícil es coger perspectiva y responder a una cuestión fundemantal: ¿Cómo ha cambiado en los últimos años el esfuerzo que debemos asumir los españoles cuando queremos adquirir una casa? ¿Es mayor o menor que en el resto de la UE? Eso es lo que ha querido aclarar el Banco de España.
¿Y qué ha averiguado? Que ese esfuerzo económico se ha disparado en los últimos 45 años. Y (lo más interesante) lo ha hecho mucho más rápido que en la media de la OCDE, la eurozona y algunos de nuestros vecinos más próximos.
Para ser más precisos, el Banco de España (BdE) estima que entre 1980 y 2025 el sacrificio necesario para acceder a una vivienda en propiedad se ha incrementado un 88,6%. Es casi nueve veces más que la media de la zona euro (10%) o Francia, donde el incremento acumulado con respecto a comienzos de los años 80 es de apenas el 9,1%. En otros países vecinos incluso se ha registrado un retroceso, caso de Alemania o Italia, que han visto cómo mejoraba la accesibilidad.
¿Cómo lo ha calculado? Teniendo en cuenta dos factores. Los cambios en la renta disponible de los hogares y la evolución de los precios de la vivienda. A lo largo de los últimos 45 años ambos han aumentado, aunque a velocidades muy dispares: el primero (renta) lo hizo mucho más lento (1,8) que el segundo (3,5). Si analizamos el conjunto de la zona euro encontramos con un escenario distinto: el dinero que tienen en el bolsillo las familias creció menos que los precios de la vivienda, pero ese desacople fue muy inferior al español (1,6 frente al 1,8).
"El deterioro relativo del indicador de acceso potencial a la vivienda en propiedad en España es, en una perspectiva histórica desde 1980, mayor que el registrado en el conjunto de la OCDE y de la UEM y mayor que el de las grandes economías europeas", resume el BdE en su último informe anual, en el que recuerda que, si bien gran parte de las economías europeas presentan problemas de acceso a la vivienda, en España las condiciones se han "endurecido en mayor medida".
¿Cuál es la razón? El organismo analiza los datos desde una perspectiva histórica. Primero recuerda que el esfuerzo necesario para adquirir una vivienda disminuyó hasta la adhesión de España a la CCE, en 1986. A partir de ese año y hasta 1991 ese indicador aumento de forma significativa y, tras varias etapas de estabilización y acelerones, alcanzó su pico en 2007, en plena burbuja.
"El ajuste en el mercado inmobiliario español dio lugar a una significativa reducción del esfuerzo para adquirir una vivienda hasta 2015, momento en el que se inicia una fase de recuperación en la que los precios crecen en mayor cuantía que la renta disponible de los hogares", reflexiona el BdE. A modo de referencia, el sacrificio que deben asumir las familias españolas para adquirir una vivienda sigue por debajo (18,1%) de 2007, pero es un 40% superior al de los 90.
¿Puede irse más allá? Sí. Que el mercado inmobiliario español se haya recrudecido mucho más que el de la UE (al menos si atendemos al esfuerzo que soportan las familias) se explica por varios factores. Uno, fundamental y del que lleva tiempo advirtiendo el BdE, es el desacople entre oferta y demanda.
En nuestro país se generan hogares a mucha más velocidad de lo que se construyen casas para alojarlos, lo que, según cálculos del regulador, ha generado un déficit de 750.000 viviendas. La falta de oferta se está agravando además en puntos muy concretos de España, como Madrid, Barcelona o Alicante.
¿Es importante eso? Sí. En cierto modo, explica la subida de precios y que a día de hoy los hogares deban destinar más de un tercio de sus ingresos a pagar su casa. El BdE calcula que las familias que no residen en viviendas de su propiedad necesitan casi siete años de renta neta para adquirir una, un dato que se eleva si hablamos de hogares con rentas más humildes, como migrantes o jóvenes.
En la ecuación por supuesto entran otros factores, como la escasez de vivienda protegida, la falta de suelo urbanizable en las ciudades, obstáculos burocráticos o la fuga de vivienda hacia mercados más rentables, como el alquiler turístico. La conclusión es en cualquier caso la misma, como recoge el BdE: el esfuerzo que deben asumir hoy los españoles para convertirse en propietarios de su casa ha crecido mucho más que el asumido por la mayoría de sus vecinos europeos.

articles.title: Comprar iPhone 18 Pro y Pro Max: el robo que muchos hackers crearon para suplantar a Apple
articles.text:
Las falsas páginas de reserva del iPhone 18 Pro pueden multiplicarse antes de la presentación esperada de Apple y copiar el aspecto de la tienda de la compañía para capturar datos personales y bancarios. Los delincuentes aprovechan anuncios de preventa, sorteos y programas de prueba para dirigir a los usuarios hacia formularios donde solicitan pagos o información sensible.
El riesgo cobra relevancia en América Latina, donde el phishing mantiene una presencia constante. La empresa de seguridad digital, Kaspersky, registró en la región un promedio de 3,5 millones de ataques diarios durante el último año, una cifra que muestra la escala de estos engaños. Los lanzamientos tecnológicos generan una oportunidad para los ciberdelincuentes porque combinan expectativa, urgencia y el deseo de conseguir un producto antes que otras personas.
PUBLICIDAD
Estafas imitan el diseño de la Apple Store
La llegada del iPhone 18 Pro y el iPhone 18 Pro Max puede impulsar la circulación de páginas que reproducen logos, colores, fotografías y estructuras similares a las de la tienda oficial de Apple. El objetivo consiste en reducir la desconfianza inicial del visitante para que introduzca sus datos sin comprobar la dirección web.
Estas campañas pueden aparecer en anuncios de redes sociales, correos electrónicos, mensajes de texto, publicaciones en foros o enlaces enviados por aplicaciones de mensajería. Algunos mensajes prometen acceso exclusivo a una reserva, un descuento limitado o la posibilidad de recibir el teléfono antes de su lanzamiento oficial.
PUBLICIDAD
El método no requiere que el sitio falso tenga un diseño deficiente. Por el contrario, los delincuentes pueden replicar elementos visuales conocidos, incluir imágenes del dispositivo y usar textos que parecen propios de una promoción legítima. La diferencia suele estar en la URL, en las peticiones de información o en las condiciones que presenta la supuesta oferta.
Probar el iPhone 18 antes de su lanzamiento: la nueva estafa
Otra modalidad consiste en invitar a los usuarios a convertirse en “probadores” del nuevo iPhone. La propuesta suele ofrecer un equipo anticipado a cambio de completar un registro, facilitar una dirección de envío y pagar una tarifa de entrega.
PUBLICIDAD
El teléfono nunca llega. La persona puede perder el dinero enviado y, además, entregar nombre completo, correo electrónico, teléfono, domicilio y datos de pago. Esa información puede utilizarse después para campañas de spam, intentos de fraude dirigidos o nuevas páginas de phishing con mensajes personalizados.
El antecedente está en septiembre de 2025, tras la presentación del iPhone 17. La compañía de seguridad detectó campañas que usaban falsas preventas, sorteos y programas para usuarios de prueba. Los engaños buscaban obtener información personal y financiera o inducir a pagos por productos inexistentes.
PUBLICIDAD
La expectativa por el iPhone 18 Pro facilita que esas fórmulas reaparezcan. La promesa de conseguir un dispositivo sin costo, reservarlo antes que el resto o participar en una experiencia exclusiva puede hacer que una oferta irreal parezca creíble.
Los mensajes fraudulentos suelen utilizar frases como “últimas unidades”, “reserva disponible por pocas horas”, “confirmación inmediata” o “has sido seleccionado”. Esas expresiones pretenden provocar una reacción rápida y evitar que la persona revise la autenticidad de la página.
PUBLICIDAD
Una promoción que exige contraseña, códigos de verificación, datos bancarios o un pago para acceder a un premio debe considerarse una señal de alerta. Los sorteos legítimos no suelen pedir información financiera antes de confirmar la participación ni condicionan la entrega de un regalo a una transferencia.
Cómo evitar una página clonada del iPhone 18 Pro
Antes de reservar un dispositivo o participar en una promoción, conviene aplicar estas medidas:
- Revisar la dirección web y detectar letras cambiadas, palabras añadidas o dominios extraños.
- Evitar enlaces recibidos por mensajes, anuncios o correos no solicitados.
- Entrar a la Apple Store desde la aplicación o escribir la dirección oficial en el navegador.
- Desconfiar de ofertas que prometen productos gratuitos, acceso anticipado o descuentos fuera de lo habitual.
- No compartir códigos de verificación, contraseñas, números de tarjeta ni documentos personales.
- No realizar pagos para recibir un supuesto premio o participar en una prueba.
- Utilizar herramientas de seguridad actualizadas para identificar sitios maliciosos.
La prevención comienza antes de pulsar un enlace. Ante promociones que apelan a la urgencia, la exclusividad o la gratuidad, revisar la dirección web y acudir a los canales oficiales permite evitar pérdidas económicas y el robo de información. La cautela sigue siendo la herramienta más efectiva frente a estafas que se apoyan en la apariencia de sitios conocidos.

articles.title: iPhone Duo pode não ser o único dobrável da Apple • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
iPhone Duo pode não ser o único dobrável da Apple
Decisão pelo nome "Duo" em vez do "Ultra" teria sido tomada pensando em versões futuras, diz jornalista.
O iPhone Duo chegou na semana passada, e se você acompanhou os rumores sobre o aparelho, sabe que ele tinha outros possíveis nomes. A decisão final, que veio a público nos 45 do segundo tempo, pode estar relacionada a uma vontade da Apple de expandir para uma linha completa, com outras opções de dobráveis.
De acordo com o jornalista Mark Gurman, conhecido por antecipar informações da companhia, a Apple planeja trazer mais iPhones dobráveis futuramente. Por isso “Duo”: é um nome que facilitaria a inclusão de outros complementos.
Gurman afirma que a Apple pode trazer uma versão maior, o suposto Duo Max, uma menor, apelidada de Duo Mini, e até mesmo uma versão de entrada, algo como um iPhone Duo SE. Perceba que os “sobrenomes” parecem muito mais naturais aqui do que um “iPhone Ultra Max”.
Caso a empresa decida por seguir esse caminho, poderia criar rivais para outras opções da Samsung, por exemplo. Na última janela, a empresa já trouxe um Galaxy Z Fold 8 em formato de passaporte (o mesmo adotado pela Apple nessa versão base) e um Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, seguindo o design anteriormente usado como padrão, em barra.
Possivelmente irritando os fãs da sul-coreana, que comercializa smartphones dobráveis há sete anos, Gurman também acredita que a empresa da maçã se tornará “predominante no mercado” e, ao mesmo tempo, force o resto da indústria “a aumentar os investimentos na categoria”.
Apresentado oficialmente pela Apple no dia 9 de setembro, junto com a linha do iPhone 18 Pro, o iPhone Duo marcou a estreia da fabricante no segmento. O modelo adota a proporção mais curta, chamada de “passaporte”, e traz um corpo construído em titânio.
Na parte de displays, o dispositivo conta com uma tela externa de 5,4 polegadas e abre-se em um painel interno dobrável OLED de 7,6 polegadas com acabamento antirreflexo em nano-textura, o que contribuiu muito para a redução da visibilidade do vinco.
A ficha técnica reúne o processador Apple A20 Pro, um conjunto de câmeras duplo com sensor principal de 48 MP na traseira, uma câmera frontal de 12 MP. A interface do iOS 27 foi adaptada para as novas proporções de tela.
No mercado brasileiro, o iPhone Duo tem pré-venda marcada para começar em 16 de outubro de 2026, com início das entregas e chegada às lojas a partir de 23 de outubro. Os preços oficiais divulgados pela Apple são:

articles.title: Underwater solar power sounds impossible, these new perovskite cells make it work anyway
articles.text:
Sunlight from the Deep: A team of Chinese researchers has developed a novel approach to solar power generation in environments where sunlight is scarce. Perovskite solar cells can be treated to operate underwater, with surprisingly good results in terms of reliability and endurance.
A newly published study describes a "robust" strategy for reliably generating power underwater. Several Chinese researchers developed a new type of submerged perovskite solar cell that can operate a few meters below sea level and harvest solar energy for years while retaining high efficiency.
In recent years, perovskite-based cells have essentially hijacked research efforts focused on new solar power breakthroughs. First discovered in 1839 beneath the Ural Mountains in Russia, perovskite is a highly flexible class of compounds that is used in ultrasound machines, memory chips, solar cells, and more.
Moisture can have a destructive impact on perovskite cells, but the Chinese researchers have apparently found a way to make their underwater setup run reliably and efficiently for years. The team "tweaked" the chemical mixture of the perovskite cells, producing a material that can both absorb the dim wavelengths reaching the seafloor and withstand degradation in seawater.
The tweaked perovskite cells are also covered by a water-repelling layer, which should help keep moisture-related degradation in check. By using larger crystal configurations, the perovskite compound can also limit the material's breakdown and improve electricity production.
The researchers first tested the new material at a simulated ocean depth of 10 meters, where it was able to convert around 35% of the dim light into electricity. Meanwhile, silicon-based solar panels can usually convert around 20% of surface sunlight into electricity. According to the in-lab tests, the new panels could retain most of their original efficiency for more than five years.
After the lab tests, the team brought the new perovskite panel to the South China Sea. The cells were mounted on a small submarine device designed to reach and maintain a specific depth. The device also included some coin-cell batteries to test the panel's ability to actually generate electricity.
The researchers tested the perovskite compound at two meters, six meters, and 10 meters below sea level. They discovered that power generation fluctuated significantly at around two meters but became more consistent at greater depths. At 10 meters, the panel was able to generate less than a quarter of the electricity it generated eight meters above.
Despite the harsh environment and dim light conditions, the researchers think their new perovskite cells could one day solve the "challenge" of harvesting solar energy underwater. The study describes some hypothetical scenarios where this kind of power generation could be useful, including autonomous marine power systems and submerged Internet of Things infrastructure.

articles.title: Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is incredibly ambitious but frustratingly bloated
articles.text:
“Ugh… The scale of all this… I’m starting to get a headache.”
Leda, one of the protagonists of Intelligent System’s Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave, makes this comment late into the strategy RPG’s campaign. She’s referring to the cataclysmic threat posed by the main villain, the demon king Balor, but incidentally, it’s also the perfect description of how I feel towards Fortune’s Weave as a whole.
While the game has a staggeringly intricate structure that weaves between three distinct arcs, the breadth and depth of all of its content proves to overbearing. The overall gameplay loop and some individual narrative beats certainly shine, but they’re unfortunately bogged down by copious amounts of excess. The end result is an entertaining, but wildly uneven, strategy-RPG experience.
A sprawling, but unfocused, epic
Right off the bat, Fortune’s Weave positions itself as a rather novel entry in the Fire Emblem series. That’s because it’s set in the same universe as 2019’s Three Houses but takes place hundreds of years later in a different land across the sea. Truthfully, it initially feels a bit like dangling keys in front of Three Houses fans, with the game opening with the Progenitor God Sothis (a returning Cassandra Lee Morris) once again teeing up your journey. But otherwise, this is entirely standalone from Three Houses.
That standalone nature is not inherently a bad thing, to be sure, although those inherent connections do make the story here feel comparatively trite. While Three Houses focused on the Game of Thrones-esque conflict between clans and a sympathetic villain who aimed to end this violent, prejudicial cycle, Fortune’s Weave is simply about the world-ending monster Balor. The game begins in this post-apocalyptic future he’s brought about, with protagonist Eshmel being sent back in time five years to change the fate of four “Flame Lords” who will aid in humanity’s last ditch effort to survive.
This is where Fortune’s Weave‘s ambition really comes to bear, as each Flame Lord, quite impressively, has their own full-sized campaign. Leda, the character I started with because of her unique musical abilities, is a minstrel who seeks vengeance for her father’s murder. Theodora, meanwhile, must take over her kingdom once her own father is killed, while Cai, a young boy, seeks to save his father from imprisonment. (Fortune’s Weave really likes paternal motivations, apparently.) And the fourth and final Flame Lord, Dietrich, is simply in it for the love of the game as he roams the land to find worthy opponents.
They all come to Dagda, a bustling Greco-Roman city, to take part in the Heroic Games, a coliseum-style tournament in which the winner is granted one wish by the church of state. And once you complete Part I of a given campaign, that Flame Lord and their allies and gear can be brought into two additional Parts, the middle of which directly segues into the final Balor section. It’s a riveting hook, especially if you play with Permadeath enabled as I did, as it feels genuinely rewarding to have successfully levelled up and guided these characters throughout the entire campaign. (And, similarly, this makes it all the more devastating should you lose any units along the way.)
There are several weaknesses within this years-spanning epic, however. For one, Balor is the most generic of apocalyptic threats, while Eshmel (who you can customize as male or female) is a practically voiceless avatar with no actual personality or dimension. As such, you simply have no attachment to either character, which causes the late stretch of the game, which took me 20-plus hours, to really suffer. Worse still, their conflict feels so jarringly disconnected from the Heroic Games. You go from a character-driven narrative with relatively low stakes (all while a larger Dagdan conspiracy is teased but never fully fleshed out) to a cataclysmic battle against a dime-a-dozen creature that really has nothing to do with the Flame Lords.
But even ignoring the Eshmel-Balor side of the game, the first two parts that lead into it are inconsistent at best. As Leda, I spent around 40 hours during the Tournament Arc, and this features a pretty rote story about the corrosive, maddening nature of revenge that also unfolds at a glacial pace due to its repetitious “match, break, match, break” structure, with plot developments being slowly drip-fed in between. Worse still, Leda’s campaign in Part II (the “War Arc”) suddenly makes her a supporting character to Theodora as the latter’s people engage in a deadly conflict with another kingdom. It’s a baffling decision to effectively reduce Leda’s role to a glorified cameo in her own story to shift focus for 10 or so hours to another protagonist in whom we have no investment.
This proves especially frustrating because the game’s insistence on making everything so elongated means that switching to going through Theodora’s campaign isn’t something you can quickly do. To be clear, I love the multiple campaigns of games like Nier Automata and Kingdom Hearts Birth by Sleep because they’re manageably sized, taking around 10 hours each and, thus, allowing me to see the bigger narrative picture in a reasonable amount of time. Fortune’s Weave, though, seems to want to punish you for not dedicating another 40 hours at least just to see other highly relevant perspectives. It feels like the Marvel Cinematic Universe at its worst, making you do “homework” with seemingly unrelated stories so you’re properly prepared for the one you actually came to see.
And of course, I can really only speak for Leda and the several hours I subsequently played of Theodora’s story, the latter of which did admittedly seem more interesting than simply “vengeance” due to its focus on the religious discrimination experienced by the nascent queen and her people. Given the staggeringly massive scope of Fortune’s Weave, I simply wasn’t able to check out Cai or Dietrich’s individual campaigns, with my only real engagement with them coming instead through incidental appearances they make during Leda’s Tournament Arc.
Perhaps the other three campaigns would have felt more cohesive (either in terms of connecting to Balor or even just standing on their own instead of this heavy MCU-like crossover), but to fully answer that question, I’d have had to play at least 200 hours before writing this review, which is simply ridiculous. Fortune’s Weave simply doesn’t respect your time.
Excellent strategy buried under lots of repetition
This sense of disjointedness extends well beyond narrative, although it takes a while for it to settle in, as Fortune’s Weave does indeed provide a legitimately engrossing gameplay loop at its core. In between tournament matches, you have an allotted number of in-game days to prepare in various ways, including by taking part in Dagdan activities like training or performances to raise stats and Bonds between allies.
The most meaningful element of Fortune’s Weave‘s calendar system, though, is the world map. Rather than being an open-world setting, you can move your character along this grid-like chart a few spaces at a time, with one turn passing along the way to inch you closer to the looming tournament match. At first, this might seem like a limitation, but I quickly came to appreciate just how much more conscientious I became about how I was spending my time.
To complete sidequests, including the character-specific ones (in Leda’s case, reaching various towns to perform music), I had to carefully plan my route for maximum efficiency, taking into account obstacles like enemies and shifting environments (i.e. a desert that slows your traversal) and making full use of carriages that offer limited fast travel opportunities. It adds to the strategic ethos at the heart of Fire Emblem in a thoughtful way.
The world map is also vast enough to encourage exploration, as venturing off the main paths may unlock hidden villages, little areas with rare loot or even dungeons. That last element is especially worth your while.
In a welcome return from the excellent 3DS game Fire Emblem Echoes: Shadows of Valentia, dungeons are 3D environments that you can fully run around in to find chests and resources. Enemies can also be struck to give you a leg up in battles, which are represented here through Clashes, Final Fantasy-esque turn-based battles with a row of party members instead of Fire Emblem‘s signature bird’s eye view, tile-based combat. All in all, dungeons offer a refreshing change of pace, although their relatively copy-and-paste visual design and layouts leave much to be desired. (Get ready to see lots of uninspired, run-of-the-mill caves.)
And because the world map exploration is so full of rewards, the classic turn-based battles feel that much more impactful. I put in all of that work to acquire that extra gear, level up that character or complete that particular sidequest, and so I would head into fights feeling gratifyingly prepared. This is especially important because Fortune’s Weave has an annoying tendency to constantly throw many (often respawning) enemies at you in story battles, even on Normal difficulty, which I inevitably switched back to from Hard in Part III, the “Salvation Arc,” due to how unrelenting it became.
I am happy to report, if nothing else, that the one major new combat gimmick that Fortune’s Weave introduces is rather brilliant. Enter Blaze Arts, which are special Flame Lord moves that cost HP in exchange for huge benefits. Leda, for instance, can strum her vihuela instrument to dramatically buff allies and even clear environmental hazards, while Theodora is able to hurl chunks of the earth for long-range attacks.
Use enough of these moves (or special high-level weapons), and you’ll enter Overblaze, a super-powered state that increases your strength, but use too many and you’ll Burst, reducing your maximum HP for the rest of the fight. It’s a brilliant risk-reward mechanic, challenging you to let it rip at the right moment lest you weaken your central units too early.
With all of that said, the nature of Fortune’s Weave, segmented as it is by four campaigns, means that there’s only a handful of actually developed characters throughout. This means that the vast majority of the units that you’ll recruit to fill out your party are painfully thin. As you run around Dagda, you’ll encounter people who will join your cause, provided you meet arbitrary criteria like sharing a minimum Bond level with them (raised by inviting them to local activities like going to meals or shows together) or high enough Renown (a gauge that increases by completing sidequests and other activities on the world map).
But despite those hefty requirements to unlock them, they don’t actually have any fleshed-out narrative of their own, practically no backstory and certainly no Support conversations to speak of. Not even Seteth, the saintly warrior who returns from Three Houses as a recruitable character, has any actual scenes with the Flame Lords, Eshmel or any of the other cast. It feels almost insulting to force you to grind so much to recruit that one character, and then they don’t have any unique story material besides a few canned lines, making them feel interchangeable and even disposable. People bemoaned the heavy social elements in Three Houses, but those, at least, always felt meaningful because all of the students and teachers had their own backstories and Support conversations to make them feel like living, breathing people as well as combat units.
The limited characterization in Fortune’s Weave proves especially glaring should you complete special Paralogue sidequests for some of the Flame Lords or their close allies in other campaigns. Doing so actually allows you to let them join you in the Salvation Arc even if you didn’t complete their campaigns, which feels like the rare time Fortune’s Weave actually forgives you for not doing everything. But even then, it leads to these hilarious MCU-esque guest roles in which characters like Dietrich became suddenly allied with me in the late-game even though I had zero context for who they were.
This also raises another critical issue: playing with Permadeath but not engaging with at least two campaigns severely kneecaps you. By the time I reached Part III, I had lost numerous allies (fatalities brought about, in no small part, due to playing on Hard for most of the game), and in this final stretch, the opportunities to recruit new units are limited outside of a few who join per the narrative or Paralogue completion. Your only other recourse, as the game keeps telling you, is to go back in time and guide the other Flame Lords to the future. In other words, Fortune’s Weave is, once again, punishing you for not putting at least 100 hours into the game.
All the while, the Salvation Arc feels dragged out due to its own structure. Essentially, you’re free to challenge Balor whenever, although naturally, you’ll need to be sufficiently levelled. What’s more, the Demon King summons Underworld Gates that you have to destroy within an allotted calendar period to make him more manageable in the final boss fight. None of this is inherently problematic, but as with so much of the game, it’s unnecessarily bloated. That’s because the Gates are often spread across the map, forcing you to split your units into smaller parties to divide and conquer, all while keeping one unit near Dagda to protect advancing waves of enemies.
The first or second time I had to do this, it proved quite captivating, challenging me to strategically deploy parties that were as balanced as possible while also saving a few to keep an eye on Dagda. It was a clever evolution of the earlier world map exploration that kept me on my toes. But having to do this several more times, with the gaps between the placement of the gates widening throughout and the individual map points that you have to reach to dispel barriers protecting them, just felt unbearably tedious.
Compounding this frustration is the fact the maps for Act 3’s story battles are all filled with their own unique forms of miasma, which coat many tiles with significant stat-reducing penalties that rarely even affect enemies. It’s yet another example of Fortune’s Weave being big for the sake of it, and it proved grating in those final hours.
Fortune favours the slog
Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave can be an exasperating game. For all of the meaningful ways it builds on the series’ central gameplay loop, particularly through an ingenious multi-act, cross-campaign approach to cause and effect and its densely layered world map, its insistence on maximalist game design regrettably harms the pacing, flow and RPG elements of the whole experience. Ultimately, I enjoyed the totality of the experience, but it really wore me out at times, and it leaves me begging Intelligent Systems to go with a “less is more” approach in future Fire Emblem games.
Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave launches exclusively on Nintendo Switch 2 on September 17.
