articles.title: HumanX 2026: Europe's AI moment moves from hype to execution (Sponsored) | EU-Startups
articles.text:
European AI is entering a different phase. In August, new provisions of the EU AI Act came into effect, including transparency requirements covering interactions with AI systems and certain AI-generated content.
For Europe’s startups, investors and business leaders, the conversation around AI is increasingly moving from what the technology could do to how it must be built, deployed and scaled in practice to comply not just with the new regulations, but how customers, partners and employees want to use it.
It is against this backdrop that HumanX will bring more than 2,500 AI leaders to Amsterdam from 22-24 September, convening founders, investors and executives from across the global AI ecosystem.
“Europe is having its moment with AI,” says Stefan Weitz, co-founder and CEO of HumanX. “You’ll have world-class founders building here, global companies deploying AI here and a regulatory environment that is influencing how the technology develops far beyond Europe. It requires a platform that reflects that growing influence and not just a trade show with content sold to the highest bidder.”
What Weitz is most looking forward to, however, is less about any individual keynote and more about who will be in the room.
“You’ll have the founder building the technology sitting alongside the enterprise leader trying to deploy it and the investor deciding where the next wave of value will be created,” he says. “With my investor hat on, I see these groups too often missing each other and making bad business decisions as a result. Bringing them together is where things get interesting.”
Next week’s speakers include Nikesh Arora (CEO, Palo Alto Networks), Marjan Rintel (CEO, KLM), May Habib (co-founder & CEO, Writer), Fabian Hedin (co-founder & CTO, Lovable), Jan Oberhauser (Founder & CEO, n8n), Joelle Pineau (Chief AI Officer, Cohere), Alex Kendall (co-founder & CEO, Wayve) and Susan Jones (CDO, Diageo), alongside investors including Nick Clegg (General Partner, Hiro Capital).
Moving beyond the conference model
HumanX was created by the team behind Money20/20, Shoptalk and HLTH, but its approach to programming is deliberately different from many large technology conferences.
Sessions are editorially chosen based on what our industry, customer and VC partners tell us are critical issues facing them right now, rather than sold as part of sponsorship packages, with programming focused on practical questions facing companies implementing AI.
“The test for us is pretty simple,” says Weitz. “Do you leave knowing something you can actually do differently on Monday? If you’ve spent three days at an AI conference and leave with lots of inspiration but no clearer idea what to do next, you’ve wasted your time and money and we haven’t done our job. Most other conferences just want you in a seat so they can sell bigger sponsorships.”
It’s also why HumanX runs differently to most conferences of its scale. Sessions are curated and moderated by a journalist rather than a friendly VC, and never sold – an independence that makes any presence on stage worth something.
Multiple structured programmes exist specifically to set up 1:1 meetings between participants, rather than leaving connections to chance in an exhibition hall. And the people running it have sat in the audience’s seat through other moments when everything changed, and know how to navigate one.
“We’re at the point where AI strategy is your business strategy,” says Weitz. “The gap between organisations experimenting with AI and those actually rebuilding around it is widening quickly. HumanX is about putting the people already doing that in the same room, and if you aren’t there, you’re not just a few months behind, you’re risking your own extinction.”
HumanX Amsterdam takes place next week at RAI Amsterdam from 22-24 September 2026, and EU-Startups readers can save €500 on HumanX Amsterdam passes with code HX26E_EUSTARTUPS.
The code expires at midnight CEST on 21 September, the day before the event begins. Register now to avail of this discount.

articles.title: The iPhone 18 Pro’s big camera update is all about the small gains
articles.text:
Last week, Apple announced an iPhone unlike any it has made in the past. An iPhone that has seemingly already led several other phone manufacturers to pursue entirely different designs for their flagship products. A remarkably distinct device with the kind of “I can’t believe they did that” software touches that Apple sometimes pulls off when it’s at the top of its game.
The iPhone 18 Pro’s big camera update is all about the small gains
The Pro camera’s major upgrade offers minor image quality improvements — whether or not you know what an f-stop is.
If you buy something from a Verge link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
That phone is not the iPhone 18 Pro.
The 18 Pro and Pro Max are in the unusual position of being the second-most interesting iPhones that Apple is launching this year. The foldable iPhone Duo stole the show at Apple’s launch event, but it’s not arriving until next month. In the meantime, the 18 Pro cometh, and it is extremely familiar even with a totally new hardware feature in the camera.
It is so similar to the iPhone 17 Pro that it can use the same cases. Have you used an iPhone 17 Pro? Great, you now know what it’s like to use the 18 Pro. There are no surprises, and unless you’re a truly committed smartphone photographer, no hugely compelling reason to pick an 18 Pro over a 17 Pro if you can find one on sale. It’s what we’ve come to expect from what was the flagship iPhone: excellent and utterly iterative.
Apple iPhone 18 Pro
The Good
- Manual exposure controls in the native camera app, finally
- Marginal improvements to image quality
- Photographing sunstars with a smartphone camera rules
The Bad
- $100 more expensive than last year
- Manual exposure controls are tiny
- Higher storage tiers are quite pricey
The Good
- Manual exposure controls in the native camera app, finally
- Marginal improvements to image quality
- Photographing sunstars with a smartphone camera rules
The Bad
- $100 more expensive than last year
- Manual exposure controls are tiny
- Higher storage tiers are quite pricey
Inside, the iPhone 18 Pro has a revamped thermal management design that allows its new A20 Pro chip to sustain full performance for longer, but the biggest truly new idea is inside the main camera, where Apple has added a moving aperture to control how much light hits the sensor. This is a big deal, and also a small deal, which I promise makes sense.
With a few exceptions, phone cameras have fixed apertures. Their sensors and lenses are so small that most of your scene is in focus even when you’re shooting wide open, and it’s usually best to get as much light as you can on that tiny sensor anyway. But there are some edge cases where a narrower aperture is helpful, even on a phone camera. It could also be helpful in other situations, particularly in low light, to open up the aperture even further than the iPhone’s traditional f/1.8. So Apple seems to have said, “Screw it. Let’s have it both ways,” and put in a variable aperture.
So there are really two separate things happening here. The maximum aperture is now bigger, at f/1.48 vs. f/1.8, and has the ability to get smaller, with stops available at f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4. And while both the larger and smaller apertures do offer marginal improvements to photo quality in some cases, the differences are generally marginal.
One of the reasons photographers like a wider aperture is for its ability to throw more of the background of a photo out of focus. But the small lens and sensor on a smartphone camera don’t allow for the same kind of soft background blur you get from a bigger camera system. At the iPhone’s old maximum aperture of f/1.8, most things are in focus most of the time, and going to the slightly wider f/1.48 doesn’t make a huge difference.
A bigger aperture does offer an advantage for low light photography. On a traditional camera, letting in more light allows the system to keep noise down by using a faster shutter speed, a lower ISO, or both. It’s not quite the same on a smartphone camera that’s combining multiple frames at different exposures to create the final image, but broadly the concept of “more light = better photo” holds.
Maybe because phones are already so good at coping with low light through these computational methods, the low light gains in the 18 Pro look pretty minor. If I look closely at the detail in a shot at f/1.48 versus f/1.8, I can see a difference, but it’s subtle.
The biggest advantage might be for Night Mode. At f/1.48, the system can use a slightly shorter Night Mode capture time compared to f/1.8. That’s less time you have to try and keep your hand still and less noise that the system needs to try and process out.
On the other side of the dial, a smaller aperture is useful for extending depth of field and keeping more stuff in focus, particularly if your subject is close to the camera. If you’re taking a close-up photo of a statue, at f/1.48 or f/1.8 the back part of it might look a bit soft. Stopping down to f/4 sharpens up the part in the background.
That’s helpful! But once again, you’ll find these benefits on the margins. That’s because the iPhone’s new f/1.48 maximum aperture actually equates to about f/5 on full frame in terms of depth of field, which already puts a lot of the stuff in front of and behind your subject in focus. Unless you’re really close to your subject, most things are in focus or close enough when you photograph them with a smartphone camera.
If you don’t know or care about f-stops, you’ll still get along just fine with this updated camera. By default the aperture is set to automatically adjust based on lighting conditions, and it seems to stay at f/1.8 most of the time in good lighting. The aperture does open up to f/1.48 in dim light automatically, and will close down to f/4 when taking a group photo with someone who’s standing further back. And I saw it consistently dropping down to f/4 when I was taking a photo of some close-up text. That’s a situation where f/4 will help you get more in focus and make for a potentially more usable photo. But that’s an awfully narrow set of use cases, whether you’re the kind of person who wants to take manual control over the aperture or not.
That’s the big update, and the effect is a relatively small one. But it’s not the only camera update. Friends, in the year of our Lord 2026, you can finally change the exposure controls by yourself in the iPhone camera app. Apple has added pro controls for the aforementioned aperture as well as shutter speed, white balance, and focus. There’s also the exposure compensation control that existed before, though no direct ISO adjustment, which someone coming from a traditional camera system would probably look for. But there’s enough control here for anyone who is so inclined to get a little more creative and hands-on with the stock app than ever before.
I noticed that when I was using a manual shutter speed, the results appeared to have been less processed. Apple spokesperson Stephanie Ng confirmed that the camera is indeed capturing a single frame rather than using the typical multi-frame processing. That means you lose a bit of dynamic range, though the final image will still include a gain map if there are highlights bright enough to warrant it. That’s not ideal if you’re trying to capture detail in both highlights and shadows, but on the other hand, this is one way to get the less-processed iPhone photo that some folks have been clamoring for. It’s a bit hidden, but it’s finally here.
On top of that, there’s a new set of texture controls for Photographic Styles, with the ability to add a film-inspired glow to highlight areas of your photo, overlay film grain, or soften skin. It’s another first for Apple: the ability to make your photos a little bit worse. But you know, tastefully, Film simulation modes for digital cameras are as popular as ever, and Apple is trying to catch that wave. The recently released Pixel 11 series includes so many ways to customize the look of your photos that their camera team had an escalation meeting about it. Likewise, Samsung has added any number of ways you can restyle your photo into what you envisioned it would be. After basically a decade of pushing the technological envelope year after year, the major phone manufacturers seem to be opening up to other definitions of image quality.
If you put all these updates together alongside the less-important but completely underrated addition of a first-party wrist strap (!) accessory for Apple’s own 18 Pro cases, maybe there’s something more camera than phone here. When I got my hands on the 18 Pro last week, I wondered if I could convince myself that the iPhone is a camera camera now.
I will go so far as to say that I had a better time shooting with the 18 Pro than I’ve ever had using an iPhone camera in the past. I shot sunstars peeking out behind some leaves in Battery Park. I took it to the US Open and documented the excitement of a night match at Arthur Ashe Stadium. I took a video of a sizzling fajita plate and converted it to a cinematic masterpiece* after capture. But I never forgot I was using a phone. The pro control icons are pretty small on the 18 Pro’s screen, and I had to focus just to hit them properly. I had to dismiss a spam call in the middle of a shoot. And after a morning of battery-draining photo and video shooting, it became really important to top the battery off so as not to lose my lifeline to the rest of the world. It’s a step closer, and the moving aperture is a bit closer to that dream of a phone that’s also a camera. But it’s still a phone.
*I use the term masterpiece loosely.
Apple, Google, and Samsung have each achieved their own kind of excellence in shaping what a smartphone camera can be. So it’s interesting watching them pivot to flexibility and embracing some of the flaws that are turning people on to old digital cameras. But taking photos with one of their flagship phones still feels like using a phone, whether there are moving aperture blades inside or not. One of the reasons I found the wrist strap so appealing was that it made the process of handling the phone as a camera feel more like, well, a camera. I’m hoping for the day when one of the few phone makers who sell devices in the US at scale tries something like the Xiaomi photography kits or Vivo’s telephoto lenses. That would feel like a whole new camera experience.
Apple is also using the 18 Pro to introduce something it calls Reference Image, which is a method the company has developed for verifying the authenticity of a photo taken on the iPhone. Apple will start using Google’s SynthID standard to tag photos with AI edits, but Reference Image comes at the problem from the other direction: helping people to identify which photos are real. Apple designed a new main camera sensor for the 18 Pro and Pro Max that adds encrypted data to the images it produces, so it’s limited to photos taken with the main camera on those two models. It’s complicated and clunky right now, but it also seems to be a pretty robust system with a lot of room to grow.
You need to enable it as a camera mode in the settings app in order to use it, and then actively switch the camera app to Reference mode to capture a Reference Image. The resulting image file contains the encrypted data from the main sensor, which means it’s bigger than a normal photo — a standard 4MB image I shot of a city street is an 8MB file when I shoot it in reference mode. If you send a Reference Image to someone who wants to verify that a Reference Image hasn’t been tampered with, they can push a button to send it to Apple’s Private Cloud Compute, where that encrypted data will be “developed” showing the image basically as it came off the sensor. (Apple’s metaphor here is having the original negative of a traditional film photograph.)
It’s hard to use at the moment, but the idea is that it’s almost impossible to tamper with. Apple is releasing an API for third-party developers to add an option to view reference photos when they’re attached to an image, and the company seems eager to push this into the wider ecosystem now that all of this has been announced.
There are some meaningful updates on the video side of the aisle, too. There’s updated focus tracking that uses AI to stick to a subject. It’ll even pick them up if they leave the frame briefly and come back, but in my brief testing it seems to forget about someone if they’re gone for more than a few seconds. You can also convert video footage from the main camera to Cinematic after the fact, in the same way that you can convert regular photos to portrait mode after you take them. I often wish I’d taken video in cinematic mode but I never remember to in the moment, so this is a nice update. Video files don’t appear to be vastly bigger compared to similar clips from the 17 Pro, so this doesn’t come at a big cost to your storage space, either.
And that’s no small thing. The 18 Pro and Pro Max are each $100 more this year, with the 18 Pro starting at $1,199 with 256GB of storage. But each jump in storage tier will cost you dearly — all the way up to a $2,399 version for 2TB. Likewise, the Pro Max starts at $1,299.99 with 256GB of storage and goes all the way up to $2,499 for the 2TB version.
You’re not getting nothing for that price hike. There’s a new chipset, the A20 Pro, plus an updated vapor chamber that’s supposed to move heat away from the chipset more effectively to help with sustained performance compared to the 17 Pro. I noted the phone getting pretty warm on my first few days of using it, which are usually pretty taxing as you’re going through setup, app downloads, and data indexing, but haven’t noticed it as a consistent problem.
Battery life is the eternally impossible question to answer about a phone after a week of using it. I haven’t experienced anything like a “normal day” for the past week, but I haven’t seen any surprising battery drain from the 18 Pro in my downtime, either. It survived a day of intense use during a video shoot without a recharge at any point, which is no small feat. Apple quotes a modest gain in battery life for the smaller Pro model — 36 hours of video playback, up from 33 hours on the 17 Pro. The 18 Pro Max offers a bigger increase: 45 hours of video playback compared to 39 on the 17 Pro Max. Verge editor-in-chief Nilay Patel has been testing the Pro Max, and he says it’s been lasting more than a day, although he also noted the same early setup vibes. He also points out his 17 Pro Max battery was a champ when it was new and now can’t make it through a day after a year of heavy use, so the real test here is going to come much later in this phone’s life cycle.
The real test here is going to come much later in this phone’s life cycle
The 18 Pro I’m testing uses Apple’s new in-house C2 modem, marking the first time that a Pro iPhone has shipped with an Apple-made cellular chip. It seems that the homegrown stuff has finally cleared Apple’s quality bar for inclusion at the very high end, and I can’t say I’ve found any reason to fault it over the past week. The C2 is paired with the N1 wireless networking chip, and the system overall seems quick to jump off a Wi-Fi signal when I’m in an elevator and just as eager to pick up a cell signal when I step out. Here’s hoping it’s just as quick to ditch my home Wi-Fi when I’m in the carport outside of my house trying to start GPS navigation — truly, the dream.
One other notable update here is that the Dynamic Island is smaller. On the 17 Pro, the black bar encompassed the Face ID sensor in addition to the front-facing camera. On the 18 Pro, the Face ID sensor is hidden under the regular part of the screen until that real estate is needed by the Dynamic Island. Apple went to great lengths to disguise the sensor under a unique pixel pattern that uses black pixels to allow the IR signals necessary for Face ID to pass through. Pretty cool, though I can’t say I noticed the Dynamic Island’s smaller size even a single time as I was using the phone, and jumping back to the 17 Pro’s larger Dynamic Island hasn’t bothered me. And I have yet to need three items in the Dynamic Island at one time, rather than two, but this is a new capability that exists on the 18 Pro.
Possibly an even bigger deal than the launch of a new $1,200 phone is the release of iOS 27, and with it the new-new AI Siri. We previewed it in detail earlier this summer, and it continues to impress me. Particularly, its ability to search across email and messages all at once — this keeps feeling more and more like a superpower the longer I use it. We also noted when it debuted that Siri as an AI chatbot is much less chatty and eager to keep you engaged than the likes of Gemini or ChatGPT, which is something I also appreciate the more I use it. iOS 27 has just gone fully public this week, and it will be interesting to see how people take to the new Siri. It has a lot of work to do to earn the trust of the public that it can do anything more complex than setting a timer reliably, but Siri seems to be on the right track at least. Finally.
Unlike Siri, the 18 Pro’s big hardware update is much less visible. The aperture is hard to see without the right light and the help of a macro lens. It’s as small as my thumbnail, and it’s under layers of optical glass. Most people who buy this phone probably won’t go looking for it, and that’s fine. It’s the kind of feature that can live in the background and just jump in to help here and there, unseen, when you need it. You don’t need to know what it is or how it works. Which is kind of the point of personal technology, anyway.
So why make a big deal out of such a small thing? Is the defining feature of Apple’s new phones really an iris as thin as a human hair that most people will never see? I think two things are true at once: Adding a major new hardware feature to the world’s most popular camera is notable to those of us who pay attention to such things. But it’s also beside the point.
The iPhone camera’s most important job is to always take a usable photo, by default, no matter what. This new aperture mechanism provides some benefits to that end, and on top of that, allows a more hands-on photographer access to camera controls that weren’t there before. But the first part of that mission is the most important, and the 18 Pro upholds that mandate. Most people who use this phone will never touch the aperture control, and that’s fine. They might get a picture of a menu that’s fully in focus thanks to the camera dropping down to f/4, or a night shot that’s a little more detailed thanks to a brighter maximum aperture. Otherwise, it will feel like the same camera they’ve come to expect from a Pro iPhone.
As long as you don’t expect a revolutionary new camera experience, then the 18 Pro is what it should be: a little better than the version that came before it.

articles.title: Lead Without a Ladder: How I Climbed Into Engineering Leadership
articles.text:
Transcript
Pauline Jepp: Rock climbing really seems like a solo act. That is, of course, until you fall, and then you realize it's all about the person that's on the other end of the rope. When I first started climbing, I thought it was a solo sport. You're the one, you're on the wall. It's a very physical puzzle that's in front of you. You're thinking about the angles of the holds, the forces, the way that you have to move. You're in the Zen moment. You're in your flow. Any climber will tell you that you don't get very far on your own. For a start, if you fall, someone's going to catch you. I don't know how familiar you all are with climbing. If you're on a rope, the person on the other end of the rope is called your belayer, and they will literally catch you when you fall.
They can quite literally save your life. If you have confidence in that person, it means that you are going to work harder, you're going to try things that you've never tried before. More than that, there's an entire community of people around about you that are willing to offer you some beta. Beta, not like software beta. I mean you are looking for some feedback to make things better, but it's those little tips, techniques, and tricks that they have learned that will help them get through the problems. Obviously, one person's beta doesn't work for everyone. We're all different heights. We have different reach. We have different strengths. We have different weaknesses, but sharing this information will help you deal with when you fall, because you will fall a lot.
There was one situation that happened very early in my climbing days, also in my early grad school days with Kaye, where I was quite new to climbing. I was inexperienced climbing something that was much harder for me than I could. My belayer was a much more experienced climber than I. I kept trying everything, and I just couldn't figure out the next move. Kept falling, she kept catching me. Just before frustration stepped in, she said, just move your feet first. It seems like a really small thing, and when I looked at the wall, I only had to move my feet like 2 inches, but those 2 inches gave me the reach I needed to grab the next hold. This has had quite a bit of an effect on me throughout my leadership journey, that balance between support and giving the beta at the right time, but also the right amount of beta. She didn't say to me, move your right foot and put it on the red hold. She just said, move your feet first, and that was enough to trigger my puzzle-solving brain to look at the things that were in front of me and to make that move.
I've had a really colorful journey to get here, not maybe one that's typical, but do any of us have a typical journey? The PhD in Canada, a research position in France for computer graphics. Lessons from Perspective Shifts
In this example, there's a number of invisible tasks. I'll talk about the invisible tasks. I think when you're moving from an IC and more and more into leadership, like whether that's even being like a tech lead, a principal engineer, technical path or managerial path, it's a different perspective. When you're a junior IC, you're focused on your code yourself. As you get more experience, you're focused on your team. Then as you get more experience, you're focusing on how you interact with another team. Then it's all the teams across the department. Then it's all the departments in the business. With every step, it's a different perspective shift and different things for you to consider. I tried to think about a few of the lessons I've had from the different perspective shifts that I think might be interesting to share. One of those is the invisible work. As I mentioned in the example, us making sure that the engineers were sharing knowledge was invisible work.
The engineers themselves being mentors and sharing their knowledge was invisible work. How do you make that visible in that it's not something that gets lost? There's no Jira card for reduced tension. No graph we can see for conflicts that are avoided. No dashboards for saying trust built. I don't know about you, but sometimes I feel like you put in an awful lot of work into a situation and then somebody turns around and goes, what do managers even do? It's this in the background. I think we have to reframe it a little bit in a similar way to the example with the teams. It's not about ownership. It's about stewardship. It's about setting the tone. Instead of being about boundaries, fostering as much collaboration as possible. Not the gatekeeping for we can all do this together, and collectively we can make it better. In order to do that, I think you need to name the work, whether it's things like mentoring.
We had to introduce a mentor program, the tech lead responsibilities. We acknowledge that the ICs might take a productivity hit because they're going to be spending time pair programming or sharing their knowledge or whatever. Name it in ways that are visible for the engineers, for the managers, for everyone to be able to make it more visible. For the manager, I think as well to shift your scoreboard, because it is a lot about what you facilitate rather than, do the tests pass? What's your GitHub history look like? Also, I've started thinking about the quiet wins. I want the engineers to raise an orange flag before it turns into a red flag. Keeping a note of these things where we've managed to avoid it becoming a red flag. Because you don't see it unless it goes wrong, do you? You put in a lot of effort to make sure that it doesn't go wrong, and to teach it forward.
I'm going to stretch my climbing metaphor wider than I can stretch my arms maybe. I think it is like instead of climbing the route yourself, you're doing the route setting. Making sure that the work is that sweet spot between achievable and challenging for your engineers. Making sure that they are bought into the work that they need to do.
The second lesson is about managing managers. The invisible work doesn't disappear when you manage managers. It becomes a little bit recursive, because now you're doing invisible work to help people do invisible work. I think maybe in smaller companies, another side effect of it is quite often you're not just delegating tasks, but you're delegating decisions being made. One particular example that we had was, so we need a lot of events on the platform to be able to sell the tickets. One of the company OKRs was the number of events that were on the platform. The number of events on the platform doesn't really tell you anything. We can have like 50 junior football matches in Germany and it's not nearly as effective as Coldplay's new concert, as some of the Oasis, whatever. It's not nearly as effective. It should be about the quality as well as the quantity.
One of the engineering managers had this insight. Although this project had been through a couple of teams, it was all about the numbers, he wanted to pick it up and do things differently. One of the things was to throw away all the process. He didn't want to use Jira, they didn't want to use what typical, like Agile, Scrumban, whatever your favorite flavor is. They just wanted a laser focus, a couple of backenders, just focus on this and just get it done. Of course, I was a little bit wary about this, because how do you keep an eye on making sure that progress is being made, they're achieving what they need to, other than if they achieve their KPIs. Happy to say they totally smashed it, so much so that they had a strategy that in the first month, they smashed their quarterly OKRs for the numbers, and then deliberately made a decision to shift, completely pivot from the pure numbers from the quantity to the quality.
They did it. They did amazing, it was brilliant. My fingerprints are nowhere on this project. I can see now that where my influence is was that I gave them the permission to do this, gave them the space that they needed to do this, the freedom, the autonomy that they needed to do this. The alignment was the quality of the events that were on the platform. We needed to follow that through as well. The separation was that they had the psychological safety in which to do that. When I'm managing managers, there's a couple of cruxes that I have come across. A crux is the hardest part of the climb. I thought I'd talk a little bit about some of the hardest cruxes that I have had to overcome. I think in this example, you can see that you don't want your engineering managers or your leads or whatever to be clones of you. You don't want them to solve problems in the same way that you solve problems. In this example, particularly, I was a little bit nervous about him throwing away all of the processes and everything, but they completely smashed it. Absolutely did it. The second one is about the context. I have had some difficult feedback in the past about how we should just tell engineers to just do it. In my experience, that doesn't get things done any quicker. I think you want people to have ownership and to be bought into the decision and the task that they're going to do in the same way that careful planning up front and thoughtfulness about your requirements, about your scoping, de-scoping will speed the project along in the long run.
I think it's similar with getting buy-in from people to pick up projects that you want them to pick up if they're going to grab ownership of this. It does take time, and it is invisible work, but I think it's worthwhile in the long run. I've learned the hard way where people, they spend so much time and effort saying, why are we doing this? Why are we doing this? Why are we doing this? When they should be using their considerable brain power to just solve the problem and get it out of the way quickly, because it would go a lot quicker if you stopped spending all that energy asking why. Share that context early and deeply. The last one is about the rescue reflex. I think this is where part of the invisible work and getting to know your engineers and professionally, what are their intellectual itches that they like to scratch?
Indeed, what are the things that they really hate to do? What do they think that are really boring? What do they not find satisfying? You get in there by having this understanding of your engineers and how their minds work. You don't want to micromanage, you don't want to get involved too early, but equally you don't want to wait until it's burning and you have to put a fire out. Another thing that's interesting with founders, especially founders that are still makers, like albeit they're 10Xers.

People just keep saying you're going to hate it, but actually, I'm quite resilient, and I just like solving interesting problems.

articles.title: For the first time, the US military confirms it has deployed weapons in orbit
articles.text:
A US Space Force Guardian monitors a space effects command and control display at the Combined Space Operations Center at Vandenberg Space Force Base, California, on May 28, 2026.
Credit:
US Space Force/David Dozoretz
A US Space Force Guardian monitors a space effects command and control display at the Combined Space Operations Center at Vandenberg Space Force Base, California, on May 28, 2026.
Credit:
US Space Force/David Dozoretz
Air Force Secretary Troy Meink made the first public declaration Monday that the United States has placed “space control weapons” in orbit, an announcement that will surely reverberate in the power centers of Beijing and Moscow.
Space Force officials have previously expressed their interest in acquiring space-based weapons, and Pentagon leaders have become more open to discussing space warfare in recent years. Therefore, Meink’s announcement Monday at the Air and Space Forces Association’s annual Air, Space & Cyber Conference near Washington, DC, was not entirely unexpected.
“Today, we continue to ensure we remain ready to meet the challenges of evolving threats, wherever they exist. This is why the United States now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action,” Meink said in prepared remarks.
Meink did not reveal any details about the weapons, but the disclosure of their existence underlines a remarkable turnaround in the Pentagon’s thinking about orbital warfare, something no senior official wanted to discuss publicly until a few years ago. Military officials recently have openly discussed orbital combat, defensive countermeasures on satellites, and a new ground-based weapon designed to disable an enemy satellite in orbit.
“There are a lot of factors that roll into how we talk about these things,” Meink said. “We spend a lot of time talking about how we’re going to talk about these things. It is important from a deterrence perspective. But on the other hand, me talking about the details of what we’re doing would actually not benefit deterrence, so we’re not going to talk about the specifics of what we’re doing, whether we’ve tested it, not tested it, or anything else.”
Meink also did not say when the Space Force deployed the space-based weapons. The development of space technology often takes years, so it is likely the weapons program, whatever it is, spanned multiple presidential administrations.
“I would just say that the space environment is critical for military and economic security, and we need to make sure that the US can operate freely there,” Meink said.
Air Force Secretary Troy Meink speaks Monday at the Air and Space Forces Association’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference in National Harbor, Maryland.
Credit:
Craig Hudson/Air and Space Forces Association
Air Force Secretary Troy Meink speaks Monday at the Air and Space Forces Association’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference in National Harbor, Maryland.
Credit:
Craig Hudson/Air and Space Forces Association
Taking stock
The Pentagon’s acknowledgment on Monday comes after US officials began highlighting Russia’s testing of an apparent anti-satellite weapon in orbit in 2020. Officials in the Biden administration accused Russia in 2024 of deploying operational anti-satellite weapons. Rep. Mike Turner (R-Ohio), the former chair of the House Intelligence Committee, revealed a US government assessment the same year that Russia might put a nuclear weapon into space. A nuclear detonation in low-Earth orbit would jeopardize thousands of commercial and military spacecraft, including Starlinks, US spy satellites, Chinese satellites, and the International Space Station.
China, too, has deployed satellites that US military officials view with suspicion. Open source data indicate Chinese satellites routinely maneuver close to US military assets in orbit, likely for surveillance, similar to the way US satellites sometimes park themselves next to Chinese or Russian spacecraft.
“China continues to launch and operate highly maneuverable satellites, demonstrating an advanced level of technological and operational acumen that, if not already deployed for such purposes, could enable a formidable on-orbit counterspace arsenal,” analysts at the Center for Strategic and International Studies wrote in their 2025 Space Threat Assessment.
In a press conference later on Monday, Meink defended the US military’s deployment of space-based weapons by citing China’s and Russia’s own advancements in the field.
“Is there any question in the room, by anybody, about whether or not the Chinese or Russians have been developing these sorts of weapons?” Meink said in response to a reporter’s question. “For over a decade, we’ve been talking about the fact, and we have expressed concern, that the Chinese and Russians were developing weapons for space. We need to focus on making sure we can protect ourselves operating in that environment.”
Military commanders have routinely used satellites for communications, navigation, and missile warning for decades. Today, the list of applications is expanding, with space-based sensing and targeting, broadband connectivity through networks like Starlink, and perhaps soon, space-based interceptors for missile defense.
The first Next-Generation Overhead Persistent Infrared (Next-Gen OPIR) missile warning satellite, estimated to cost more than $4 billion, is likely the Space Force’s most expensive satellite since the branch was established in 2019.
Credit:
Lockheed Martin
The first Next-Generation Overhead Persistent Infrared (Next-Gen OPIR) missile warning satellite, estimated to cost more than $4 billion, is likely the Space Force’s most expensive satellite since the branch was established in 2019.
Credit:
Lockheed Martin
“With everything we’re talking about doing, from long-range fires to control of our forces, our maintaining and being able to count on those space capabilities is important,” Meink said. “It is critically important that we maintain our dominance, not only in the air but in space. So we’ve had to take steps to make sure that when we’re threatened, we can take care of that.”
President Donald Trump nominated Meink for the top civilian post in the Air Force last year. Before becoming secretary, Meink served as an Air Force officer, civilian program manager, and senior intelligence official in Democratic and Republican administrations.
The categories include directed-energy, such as lasers, radio frequency jammers, and kinetic weapons capable of physically destroying a target. These types of weapons could be positioned on the ground or in space. In 2025, Gen. Chance Saltzman, until earlier this month the Space Force’s chief of space operations, said other countries, presumably China and Russia, are pursuing all six categories. “We’re not pursuing all of those yet,” Saltzman said at the time.
But Saltzman argued that maybe the United States should. “There are good reasons to have all those categories,” he said.
The Space Force revealed its first acknowledged weapon system in June, when it announced the operational acceptance of a ground-based mobile satellite jammer called Meadowlands. Victoria Samson, chief director of space security and stability at the Secure World Foundation think tank, speculated that the “space control weapons” announced by Meink on Monday could be jammers placed in orbit.
“China and Russia are both thought to have space-based jammers,” Samson wrote in an email to Ars. “I’ve always thought that the US must have them, too.”
Anti-satellite tests, particularly those using direct ascent or other kinetic weapons, have been widely condemned because they generate space debris.
Anti-satellite tests, particularly those using direct ascent or other kinetic weapons, have been widely condemned because they generate space debris.
Credit:
NASA
US officials have repeatedly voiced a preference for “counterspace” weapons that do not generate space debris. A space-based kinetic weapon would leave behind a cloud of space junk, jeopardizing countless satellites in orbit, including the US military’s own assets, and there’s no public indication that the United States has tested such a weapon (the US military has demonstrated a ground-based anti-satellite weapon), according to Clayton Swope, deputy director of the Aerospace Security Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
“Then there are non-kinetic weapons such as signal jammers and spoofers and laser dazzlers. From an under-the-hood hardware standpoint, such weapons are doppelgängers to technology already found at scale in orbit,” Swope said. “Any radio transmitter could be a jammer. Any inter-satellite optical link could be a laser dazzler. Certainly, a jammer or dazzler could be purpose-built, too.”
It is also not clear what the US military’s space weapons might target. Space control has a broad definition in US military doctrine, and the term encompasses weapons that could be used against targets in space or on Earth, Swope said.
“For example, blowing up a satellite ground station to prevent an adversary from using a satellite is a space control activity,” Swope told Ars. “The fact that the weapons—plural—are on-orbit is a more significant data point and disclosure. This might be the first time a US official has spoken about the United States possessing on-orbit weapons.”
Swope said the lack of detail in Meink’s statement Monday raises questions about the Pentagon’s motivation for the disclosure.
“It is too vague to have a meaningful deterrent value,” Swope said. “Deterrence is not only about a weapon’s fact of existence but also about having an awareness of how the weapon will be used. For example, the concept of mutually assured destruction was based on the premise of how nuclear weapons would be used and not simply the fact of their existence.
“What also made deterrence work is an awareness of the destructive power of nuclear weapons,” Swope continued. “Both how and when the [space-based] weapon would be used and its destructive potential are ambiguous. Talking heads and pontificators like me are going to have a field day with the disclosure, but it’s not clear what Russia, China, and other potential adversaries are supposed to do with it.”
There was no immediate reaction Monday from the governments of China or Russia.
“Now that the United States has officially acknowledged it has those systems in space, it has opened the door for China and Russia to do the same, which people in the US will then use as justification for why we needed those systems there in the first place,” Samson said.
What is clear is there is now an arms race in orbit. The United States and China are leading the way by measures of volume and sophistication, while Russia appears to be the most aggressive in terms of tactics. But it matters less who started the arms race than how it ends.
Stephen Clark is a space reporter at Ars Technica, covering private space companies and the world’s space agencies. Stephen writes about the nexus of technology, science, policy, and business on and off the planet.

articles.title: AMD Ryzen 5 5500F Beats Ryzen 5 5500 by Up to 16% in Early Gaming Benchmarks
articles.text:
Tuesday, September 15th 2026
	
									
	
	
	
AMD Ryzen 5 5500F Beats Ryzen 5 5500 by Up to 16% in Early Gaming Benchmarks
AMD's new Ryzen 5 5500F is turning out to be more than just a rebadge of the standard Ryzen 5 5500 in gaming. New benchmarks from YouTuber RandomGaminginHD show the $99 chip pulling ahead of its non-F sibling by up to 16% in CPU-bound titles, even though both processors share the same core count and land at roughly the same price. Do note that the testing is done by a mostly unknown third-party reviewer, and we don't have solid data track to back the claim, but for now it remains as a reference for future independent reviews from traditional sources.
The testing paired both chips with an RX 9060 XT 16 GB graphics card and ran through seven games at 1080p. Battlefield 6 showed the biggest gap at 16% in favor of the new 5500F, followed by Cyberpunk 2077 at 11%, GTA V: Enhanced at 9%, and Counter-Strike 2 at 8%. Titles that leaned more on the GPU, like Crimson Desert and Red Dead Redemption 2, saw that gap shrink to single digits or vanish once the RX 9060 XT became the bottleneck instead of the CPU. Of course, these are early numbers from one single test system. The reviewer also does not have a perfect track record when it comes to quality of testing, so it's important to wait for further testing to form a concrete verdict either way.While the two chips appear to be almost identical by name, the difference comes down to what's under the hood. The 5500F uses AMD's "Vermeer" chiplet design, the same silicon found in pricier Zen 3 parts, and it gets a 200 MHz higher boost clock plus PCIe 4.0 support. The regular 5500, on the other hand, runs on the monolithic "Cezanne" die and is capped at PCIe 3.0. AMD launched the 5500F as a new entry-level pick for the decade-old AM4 platform, and it looks like Zen 3 still has some life left in it yet.

articles.title: 5 pulseiras inteligentes baratas para acompanhar seus treinos
articles.text:
Elas são básicas, mas podem ser excelentes companhias para atividades físicas: as pulseiras inteligentes não costumam contar com recursos avançados, com os encontrados em smartwatches, mas, por um preço mais em conta do que os relógios, podem ajudar a monitorar o seu desempenho em diversos tipos de exercícios físicos diferentes.
Para ajudar quem está em busca de um modelo sem gastar muito, o Olhar Digital selecionou 5 smartbands baratinhas que contam com recursos voltados para a prática de atividades físicas. Confira abaixo e aproveite para comprar a sua:
Samsung Galaxy Fit3
A Samsung Galaxy Fit3 é uma pulseira inteligente feita com caixa de alumínio e tela de 1,6 polegada. A navegação é feita por toques na tela e por um botão lateral. O modelo pesa 18,5 gramas e utiliza pulseira de silicone com encaixe de remoção rápida.
Na parte inferior, sensores ópticos fazem a leitura dos batimentos cardíacos e da oxigenação do sangue. O aparelho também conta os passos, monitora o sono e possui sensores de movimento que identificam quedas, permitindo o envio de mensagens de emergência pelo celular conectado.
A bateria tem duração estimada de até 13 dias e o carregamento é feito por cabo magnético. O dispositivo possui proteção IP68 e resistência a 5 ATM para uso em água rasa, além de exibir notificações do smartphone via Bluetooth.
Huawei Band 11
A Huawei Band 11 possui corpo de plástico e tela AMOLED de 1,62 polegada. O visor conta com sensor para ajuste automático de brilho conforme a luz do ambiente.
Os leitores na base do aparelho acompanham a frequência cardíaca, a oxigenação do sangue, o estresse e as fases do sono. O sistema inclui configurações para mais de 100 modalidades esportivas, mas necessita do GPS do celular pareado para registrar rotas ao ar livre.
O modelo é resistente à água em até 50 metros de profundidade (5 ATM). A bateria dura até 14 dias em uso moderado, possui suporte a carregamento rápido e o dispositivo é compatível com celulares Android e iPhone.
Xiaomi Smart Band 10
A Xiaomi Smart Band 10 tem formato oval com moldura de alumínio e tela de 1,72 polegada. O painel possui taxa de atualização de 60 Hz e iluminação reforçada para leitura sob luz solar. As pulseiras são presas por encaixe direto no corpo do módulo.
Os sensores traseiros registram a frequência cardíaca, o nível de oxigênio no sangue, as etapas do sono e a contagem de passos. Para treinos, o sistema oferece mais de 150 modalidades, sem antena de GPS integrada no hardware.
A bateria oferece autonomia de até 21 dias em uso básico e recarrega em cerca de uma hora via cabo magnético. A estrutura conta com vedação contra água de 5 ATM.
Tranya ES11
A Tranya ES11 é uma pulseira de entrada com caixa de plástico e tela de 1,47 polegada. O painel exibe o horário, a contagem de passos, a estimativa de calorias e os alertas de mensagens do celular.
Os leitores na parte traseira fazem a medição dos batimentos cardíacos e o registro do tempo de sono. O sistema traz opções simples para cronometrar caminhadas e corridas, sem suporte a rastreamento por GPS.
A carcaça possui certificação IP68 contra poeira e respingos de água. O recarregamento da bateria interna é feito por um cabo magnético conectado aos pinos traseiros do aparelho.
PEJE Band 1
A PEJE Band 1 possui caixa metálica e tela de 1,45 polegada. O mostrador exibe os contadores diários de movimento, a distância estimada, a hora e os avisos do smartphone.
Os componentes na base do módulo realizam a leitura da pulsação e o registro básico de exercícios. A transferência dos dados para o aplicativo e a recepção de alertas dependem da conexão Bluetooth com o celular.
A estrutura conta com proteção IP68 contra água e poeira para uso diário. A bateria interna é recarregada por cabo magnético acoplado na parte traseira do dispositivo.
